The short index is https://leadgreen.ai/llms.txt; the data is https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/. CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences.

# How much energy does an AI query use?

> One answer from a busy 32B model costs about 0.040 Wh of GPU energy; Google says 0.24 Wh per median prompt. Both are right. Here is why.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/blog/how-much-energy-does-an-ai-query-use/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/blog/how-much-energy-does-an-ai-query-use/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Blog*

By Prem Naraindas · 19 October 2026 · Lead Green, a Katonic project

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. How much energy does an AI query use?. https://leadgreen.ai/blog/how-much-energy-does-an-ai-query-use/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

Look, this is the question I get asked most, usually by someone who has just signed off a token budget. "How much energy does one of these queries actually use?" And the honest first answer is that nobody who quotes a single figure is telling you the whole story, because the number depends on four things: which model, on which GPUs, how busy the server was, and how long the answer ran. So here is the number the public measurements give, with those four things stated, and then the two figures the vendors have published, and why they are different without either being wrong.

## The number

On the index's reference row, Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, a busy server produces a million output tokens for 63.5 Wh of GPU energy. The benchmark's answers on that row averaged 634 tokens, so one answer costs about **0.040 Wh**. That is a kilowatt-hour for roughly 24,800 answers. A 10 W LED bulb uses the same energy in about 14 seconds. The bulb is my assumption, not a source; the tokens are.

Three qualifications, and they are not fine print. It is GPU energy only: the host, the network, the cooling and the building are outside it. It was measured with the server running 256 requests at once, which is a busy server. And it is one model on one card count. Change any of those and the number moves, sometimes by a lot.

## What Google and Mistral published

In August 2025 Google put the median Gemini Apps text prompt at **0.24 Wh**, 0.03 g of CO2e and 0.26 mL of water. In July 2025 Mistral put a 400-token reply from its large model at 1.14 g of CO2e and 45 mL of water, without a watt-hour figure. Those are the only two per-prompt disclosures from model vendors I know of, and I am glad they exist.

Google's 0.24 Wh is about 6× my 0.040 Wh. See, that gap is the interesting part, and it is mostly boundary. Google counts the whole stack: the accelerators are 58 percent of its figure, so about 0.14 Wh, with the host machines, idle capacity held for peaks, and the data centre's overhead making up the rest. Google also reports a narrow, accelerator-only figure of 0.10 Wh, which is the boundary this index uses. So on a like-for-like boundary its number is 3.5× mine, and the rest of the difference is a different model, a different prompt length, and a fleet running at whatever utilisation Google's traffic gives it rather than a benchmark holding a server full.

None of that makes either figure wrong. They answer different questions. Google's tells you what a prompt costs a hyperscaler across its whole estate. The index tells you what a named model on named GPUs costs at a stated load, which is the figure you can hold a vendor to, because you can measure it yourself.

## What moves it most: how busy the server is

Take the same Qwen 3 32B on the same 2 × H100 and run it with 8 requests at once instead of 256. Energy per million tokens goes from 63.5 to 452 Wh, and one answer goes from 0.040 Wh to about **0.29 Wh**. Same model, same cards, same prompts, 7.1× the energy, because the cards draw only about 39 percent more power serving two hundred and fifty people than eight, and at eight they are mostly waiting.

Think of a bakery oven. It costs about the same gas to run whether there are two loaves in it or forty. The gas per loaf is a different matter. In the deployments I see, most enterprise assistants are the oven with two loaves in it: a department, a few dozen users, a handful of requests at any moment. Their energy per answer is at the top of that range, not the bottom, and nothing on their invoice says so.

## The range

Across the whole index, the lowest row is Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on 1 × B200 at 13.0 Wh per million tokens, which is about 0.005 Wh for one of its 396-token answers. The highest configuration the benchmark measured at all, not an index row but a real run, is Llama 3.1 405B Instruct on 8 × B200 holding 8 requests: 6,073 Wh per million tokens, about 2.2 Wh an answer, 10.6× the highest index row. So "how much energy does an AI query use" has a defensible answer somewhere between a few thousandths of a watt-hour and a couple of watt-hours, and the four things above decide where.

## What I am not telling you

Closed models served over an API. Nobody outside the operator can measure them, so I say nothing about them beyond what the operator publishes, which for most of them is nothing. Water: the index measures electricity and not water; Google and Mistral both publish a water figure and I think that is the right thing to do, but neither is per million tokens at a stated load, so it stays out of the tables. And the meter: to get from a GPU figure to what the building draws, multiply by the system's host-to-GPU ratio and the site's PUE, which only the operator knows. The [method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method) works one example.

## What to do with it

If you buy tokens from a hosted API, the concurrency is theirs and you cannot measure it; ask the provider the [seven questions](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) instead. If you run the GPUs, ask your vendor for watt-hours per million output tokens at your running batch, not theirs, and hold the answer against the [model's page](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-32b/). Or ask the [MCP server](https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/) in plain words; it will give you the row, the source and the caveat, which is more than most invoices do.

*References*

1. [ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).
2. Elsworth et al., Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google Scale, Google, August 2025: 0.24 Wh, 0.03 gCO2e and 0.26 mL per median Gemini Apps text prompt; accelerators 58 percent; narrow boundary 0.10 Wh. [arXiv 2508.15734](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15734).
3. Mistral AI, Our contribution to a global environmental standard for AI, July 2025 (with Carbone 4 and ADEME): 1.14 gCO2e and 45 mL per 400-token reply. [mistral.ai](https://mistral.ai/news/our-contribution-to-a-global-environmental-standard-for-ai).
4. Per-answer figures are Wh per million output tokens multiplied by the row's own average output length; the LED bulb (10 W) is a stated assumption. Every row: [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/) and [the API](https://leadgreen.ai/api/).

# What is watt-hours per million tokens, and why not joules per token?

> The unit behind the index: what Wh/M counts, what it leaves out, how it converts to kWh, carbon and the meter, and why joules per token became watt-hours.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/blog/what-is-watt-hours-per-million-tokens/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/blog/what-is-watt-hours-per-million-tokens/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Blog*

By Prem Naraindas · 19 October 2026 · Lead Green, a Katonic project

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. What is watt-hours per million tokens, and why not joules per token?. https://leadgreen.ai/blog/what-is-watt-hours-per-million-tokens/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

Look, every table on this site is in one unit, watt-hours per million output tokens, and I get asked why. The benchmark we build on publishes joules per token. Finance thinks in kilowatt-hours. Facilities thinks in kilowatts. Sustainability wants kilograms of CO2e. So this post is the unit, start to finish: what it counts, what it leaves out, how to move between it and every other number people ask for, and why I picked it over the alternatives.

## The definition

Take the GPU energy a server used while it was serving, in joules. Divide by the output tokens it produced in the same window. That is joules per output token, which is what the ML.ENERGY benchmark measures. Multiply by a million, divide by 3,600, and you have watt-hours per million output tokens, Wh/M. One Wh/M is 0.0036 joules per token; the arithmetic never changes, so you can go back and forth without losing anything. The reference row on the index is 0.2285 J per token, which is 63.5 Wh/M.

Two words in that definition carry the weight. **GPU energy:** the cards and nothing else. The host, the network, the cooling and the building are outside the figure. **Output tokens:** the tokens the model produced, not the ones it read. The prompt still costs energy to process, and that energy is inside the figure, because the benchmark divides everything the GPUs used by the outputs alone. So Wh/M is the whole GPU bill per unit of what you got.

## Why not joules per token?

Because the numbers are hard to hold in your head. Across the index, joules per token run from 0.047 to 2.06. Those are decimals with the interesting part in the second and third place, and nobody in a capacity meeting is going to compare 0.047 with 0.2285 and feel the difference. The same rows in Wh/M are 13.0 to 572.9: whole numbers, a 44× spread you can see. The scaling is the only change; the information is identical.

The second reason is the bill. Tokens are sold by the million, and electricity is sold by the kilowatt-hour. A unit that is watt-hours over millions of tokens sits between the two invoices, which is where the question lives. See, 63.5 Wh per million tokens is 63.5 kWh per billion tokens, no conversion table needed, and that is the number a finance person can multiply by a tariff.

## Why not energy per request?

Because requests are not the same size. On the index's chat workload, the average answer runs from 462 to 1,464 tokens depending on the model; on the same leaderboard's problem-solving task, answers run 5,361 to 8,969 tokens. Energy per request is what a bill sees, and it is the right number to ask for when you are forecasting a particular product, but it mixes the model's efficiency with how talkative it is. Energy per token separates the two. When you want per request, multiply by your own average output length: the reference row's 634-token answers cost about 145 joules each, which is 0.040 Wh.

## Why not power?

Power, in watts, is what the facility engineer sees and what the feed is sized for. It is not efficiency. A card at full draw producing few tokens and a card at full draw producing many read the same on a power meter, and the difference between them is the whole point. Energy per token is power divided by throughput: watts divided by tokens per second gives joules per token, and the same scaling gives Wh/M. On the reference row that is 1,177.9 W divided by 5,155.5 tokens per second, times a million, over 3,600, equals 63.47 Wh/M. I put that identity in the RFP scoring box on the [why page](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#monday), because any bidder's figure that fails it was not measured.

## The conditions that travel with the number

A Wh/M figure without its conditions is a number without a unit. Three conditions must come with it. The **running batch**: how many requests the server was decoding at once, averaged over the window; the same model on the same cards moves 7.1× between a batch of 8 and 256. The **latency**: the median inter-token latency users were getting, 44 ms on the reference row, under the leaderboard's 500 ms ceiling. And the **boundary**: GPU only, or with the host, network and cooling, and if so how much. Every row on the index states all three. Every vendor figure you are given should too, and if it does not, ask.

## From Wh/M to everything else

- **Kilowatt-hours.** Wh/M × millions of tokens ÷ 1,000. A billion tokens at 63.5 Wh/M is 63.5 kWh.
- **Tokens per megawatt-hour**, the capacity planner's number. One MWh of GPU energy at the reference row serves 15.8 billion output tokens; at the top of the concurrency ladder, 2.2 billion. Same cards, same MWh.
- **Carbon.** Wh/M × the grid's grams of CO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000 gives kilograms per billion tokens. The reference row on Serbia's grid (668 gCO2e per kWh, Ember 2024) is 42.4 kg per billion. The grid figure is location-based and lifecycle; the [grid pages](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) say what that means for your report.
- **The meter.** Multiply by the system-to-GPU power ratio (a DGX B200 is 1.79) and the site's PUE, which only the operator knows. With an assumed PUE of 1.3, the reference row is about 148 Wh/M at the meter, 6.8 billion tokens per facility MWh. Both multipliers are assumptions in that example, and I say so every time I use it.
- **Money.** At USD 0.10 per kWh, my assumption, the reference row is 0.6 cents per million tokens. Small. The number matters because it tracks GPU-hours, which are not small.

## What the unit does not tell you

It does not tell you what your deployment uses. Every index row is a floor: the most efficient configuration measured, on a busy server, GPU only. It does not tell you about water, which the index does not measure. It does not tell you about closed models behind an API, which nobody outside the operator can measure. And it does not rank anyone as green. In my view it is the one number that ties a model, a card and a load to a feed, a bill and a carbon line at the same time, and that is the case for it. The rows are on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/), the same numbers are in [the API](https://leadgreen.ai/api/), and the [MCP server](https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/) will do the conversions above for you and repeat the caveat every time.

*References*

1. [ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).
2. Ember, Yearly electricity data, September 2026 release, emissions intensity of total generation, 2024, CC BY 4.0. [ember-energy.org](https://ember-energy.org/data/yearly-electricity-data/).

4. Conversions: Wh/M = J per token × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600; kWh per billion tokens = Wh/M; kg CO2e per billion tokens = Wh/M × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000. Method and every row: [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method).

# Why an idle GPU wastes energy: the concurrency ladder

> Same model, same two H100 cards: 7.1× in GPU energy per token between a running batch of 8 and 256. Why the under-used card is the expensive one.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/blog/why-an-idle-gpu-wastes-energy/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/blog/why-an-idle-gpu-wastes-energy/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Blog*

By Prem Naraindas · 19 October 2026 · Lead Green, a Katonic project

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Why an idle GPU wastes energy: the concurrency ladder. https://leadgreen.ai/blog/why-an-idle-gpu-wastes-energy/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

Look, when people want to cut the energy their AI uses, they reach for a smaller model or a newer card. Both work. But on the same model and the same cards there is a lever that moves the number further than a change of GPU generation does, and in the deployments I see it is the one nobody has looked at: how many requests the server is handling at once. So here is the exhibit: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, same weights, same prompts, measured by the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard at nine different loads. At a running batch of 8 it costs 452 Wh of GPU energy per million output tokens. At 256 it costs 63.5 Wh. That is 7.1× on hardware nobody touched.

## The ladder

*Qwen 3 32B, BF16, 2 × H100. ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0, Text Conversation, all nine measured configurations. The highlighted row is the index row.*

| Cap | Running batch (avg) | Wh / M | Median ITL (ms) | Tokens / s | GPU power (W) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 8 | 452.0 | 15 | 522 | 850 |
| 16 | 16 | 252.8 | 16 | 970 | 883 |
| 32 | 32 | 153.8 | 18 | 1,706 | 944 |
| 64 | 64 | 102.0 | 22 | 2,654 | 974 |
| 96 | 96 | 84.6 | 26 | 3,356 | 1,022 |
| 128 | 128 | 76.4 | 30 | 3,905 | 1,074 |
| 192 | 192 | 69.0 | 37 | 4,601 | 1,143 |
| 256 | 256 | 63.5 | 44 | 5,155 | 1,178 |
| 384 | 340 | 64.6 | 55 | 5,071 | 1,180 |

The cap is how many requests the server was allowed to hold; the running batch is how many it actually held, on average, while it was decoding. Energy per token falls the whole way to the highlighted row. Power rises, but only 39 percent, from 850 W to 1,178 W across both cards. Tokens per second rise 9.9×, from 522 to 5,155. Median inter-token latency goes from 15 ms to 44 ms, and nobody reading an answer will notice either. Energy per token is power divided by throughput, so when throughput moves 9.9× and power moves 39 percent, energy per token moves 7.1×.

## Why the under-used card costs more

A model writes one token at a time, and to write each one it has to read its whole set of weights out of the cards' memory. In plain terms, for a dense model like this one, that read is the expensive part of every step, and it costs about the same whether the step produces one token for one user or 256 tokens for 256 users. The card is a lecturer. The lecture costs the same to give to 8 people as to 256; what changes is the cost per head. See, that is why the power column barely moves while the tokens column runs away: at a batch of 8 the cards were already doing the heavy work, for very few people.

One caveat on the word idle. The benchmark never measured an empty card: every row holds at least 8 conversations, with a queue behind them. A departmental assistant with two or three requests in flight, the common case in the deployments I see, sits above the top row. Idle here means under-used, and if anything the ladder understates what under-used costs.

## Most of the gain comes early

You do not need 256 requests in flight to get most of it. By a running batch of 64 the same cards read 102.0 Wh/M, 4.4× down from the top row, at 22 ms median latency and 974 W. That is 90 percent of the whole drop, at a load one busy business unit can generate. The rest of the ladder buys the remainder, and buys it more slowly.

## Where it turns

More is not always better. At a cap of 384 the two cards read 64.6 Wh/M, a little above the best row, at 55 ms median latency, and the slowest token in a hundred now waits 240 ms against 148 ms one row up. The server was allowed 384 and held 340, which I read as the cards running out of memory for the conversations in flight: the engine starts juggling them, the users at the back feel it, and energy per token stops improving. The index takes the lowest-energy row at or under the leaderboard's 500 ms ceiling, the 256 row here, and the curve past it is why an index row is a floor and not a target.

## A small model on one card does the same

*Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, BF16, 1 × H100. ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0, Text Conversation, all eleven measured configurations. The highlighted row is the index row.*

| Cap | Running batch (avg) | Wh / M | Median ITL (ms) | Tokens / s | GPU power (W) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 8 | 126.3 | 7 | 1,070 | 486 |
| 16 | 16 | 73.0 | 8 | 1,954 | 513 |
| 32 | 32 | 45.8 | 9 | 3,391 | 560 |
| 64 | 64 | 32.9 | 12 | 5,147 | 610 |
| 96 | 96 | 28.6 | 14 | 6,260 | 644 |
| 128 | 128 | 26.4 | 16 | 7,037 | 669 |
| 192 | 192 | 23.2 | 21 | 8,223 | 688 |
| 256 | 255 | 21.3 | 26 | 9,010 | 691 |
| 384 | 383 | 20.6 | 38 | 9,248 | 687 |
| 512 | 511 | 19.5 | 47 | 9,806 | 688 |
| 768 | 691 | 19.8 | 63 | 9,603 | 685 |

Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on 1 × H100: 126 to 19.5 Wh/M, 6.5× on one card, power up 41 percent, throughput up 9.2×. 87 percent of the drop is in by a batch of 64, and past the best row, at a cap of 768, it turns the same way, holding 691 of the 768 it was allowed. A much smaller model, one card instead of two, the same shape. In my view the shape is the finding: it is a property of how these servers decode, not of one model, and every model's own ladder is on [its page](https://leadgreen.ai/models/).

## What it does to the bill

Electricity is the small part of this and I will not pretend otherwise. The number that moves a budget is GPU-hours, and the ladder is a GPU-hours table in disguise. At the top row a million output tokens takes 1.06 GPU-hours on these two cards; at the best row, 0.11. Same cards, same model, 9.9× the tokens out of every hour of silicon you rent or own. Turn it round for the facility: one megawatt-hour of GPU energy serves 2.2 billion output tokens at the top of the ladder and 15.8 billion at the index row, and a site with a fixed power envelope, which is every site, only gets to choose which of those two it is.

## What to do with it

- **Measure your running batch before you buy anything.** vLLM reports it as `num_requests_running`; average it over a busy hour. If it is in single figures you are at the top of the ladder, and no change of card on the [comparison page](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/) moves the number as far as filling the cards you have.
- **Consolidate.** Fewer, busier cards. Three teams each running their own copy of the same model on their own pair of cards is the usual arrangement I see; one shared deployment carrying all three sits rows further down this table, and it costs nothing in hardware.
- **Ask the vendor for Wh per million output tokens at your running batch,** not theirs, and put your own [N] into the RFP clause on the [why page](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/). A figure measured at 256 in flight tells you nothing about a service that will run at 8.
- **Do not chase the bottom of the table.** Past the best row the users wait and the energy does not fall. Pick the row on the [model page](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-32b/) that matches the latency you promised, and hold the vendor to it.

I think this is the table to take into the capacity meeting, because it is the lever you already hold. The full ladders, with the definitions, are on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#concurrency).

*References*

1. [ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).
2. The rows: all nine measured configurations of Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 and all eleven of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on 1 × H100, Text Conversation, BF16. Cap is vLLM's `max_num_seqs`; running batch (avg) is the average `num_requests_running` over the steady-state window; queued requests are not counted. Full ladders on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#concurrency); every model's curve is in [the API](https://leadgreen.ai/api/).
3. GPU-hours per million output tokens = cards × 1,000,000 ÷ output tokens per second ÷ 3,600. Tokens per megawatt-hour = 1,000,000 ÷ Wh/M, in millions.
4. The mechanism: Pope et al., Efficiently Scaling Transformer Inference, November 2022, [arXiv 2211.05102](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.05102), on generation at a small batch being bound by reading the weights; Kwon et al., Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention, SOSP 2023, [arXiv 2309.06180](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180), on the memory held for requests in flight limiting the batch a server can hold. The reading of the 384 row as memory running out is mine.

# What a million tokens costs in watt-hours

> What the public measurements say a million output tokens takes in GPU watt-hours, and why a busy server uses a fraction of the energy of a quiet one.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/blog/what-a-million-tokens-costs-in-watt-hours/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/blog/what-a-million-tokens-costs-in-watt-hours/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Blog*

By Prem Naraindas · 26 September 2026 · Lead Green, a Katonic project

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. What a million tokens costs in watt-hours. https://leadgreen.ai/blog/what-a-million-tokens-costs-in-watt-hours/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

Look, everybody in this industry now buys tokens. Per million, on an invoice, from a cloud or from their own GPUs. And nobody gets told what a million of them costs in electricity. I have sat in enough capacity meetings to know the question is coming, so this is the baseline: what the public measurements say a million output tokens takes in watt-hours, and what moves the number.

## The unit

Watt-hours per million output tokens, Wh/M. It is GPU energy only, divided by the tokens the model produced. Prompt processing is inside the figure, because the measurement divides total GPU energy by output tokens. Host, network, cooling and idle time are not inside it. So every number here is a floor.

For scale: a million output tokens is roughly three quarters of a million words of English. And the reference row below, 63.5 Wh, is a 2 kW kettle running for 1.9 minutes. The kettle is my assumption, not a source; the tokens are.

## Where the numbers come from

The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard, run by the ML.ENERGY Initiative (it started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan), serves open-weight models with vLLM on real H100 and B200 servers and measures GPU energy at steady state with its Zeus library. It publishes every stable configuration it ran (328 for this task) as JSON in its repository, and every run including the unstable ones in a gated Hugging Face dataset whose card declares Apache 2.0. Version 3.0 was released on 1 December 2025; the data I use was compiled on 16 February 2026. I took its Text Conversation task, kept the 328 configurations it published, and for each model and GPU picked the one with the least energy per token at or under a median inter-token latency of 500 ms, the leaderboard's own default. None of them comes near it. That gives 32 rows for 18 models. My 32 rows match the leaderboard's table when one GPU is selected at a time; at its default view it shows one row per model, 18 rows.

## Three numbers

- **Lowest: 13.0 Wh/M.** Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on 1 × B200. A small model on the newest card, kept busy.
- **Reference: 63.5 Wh/M.** Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, at a running batch of 256 and 44 ms median inter-token latency, the two cards drawing 1,178 W between them. I use this row for every carbon calculation on the site, because, in the deployments I see, a 32B dense model on two H100s is what a serious enterprise deployment looks like today.
- **Highest: 572.9 Wh/M.** Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 on 8 × H100. Eight cards to hold the weights, and every token pays for all eight.

The span from lowest to highest is 44×. That is model size and hardware generation, and it is what people expect the story to be. It is not the interesting part.

## The interesting part

Take the reference model and change nothing except how many requests the server holds at once.

*Qwen 3 32B, BF16, 2 × H100. ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0, Text Conversation.*

| Cap | Running batch (avg) | Wh / M | Median ITL (ms) | Tokens / s | GPU power (W) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 8 | 452.0 | 15 | 522 | 850 |
| 16 | 16 | 252.8 | 16 | 970 | 883 |
| 32 | 32 | 153.8 | 18 | 1,706 | 944 |
| 64 | 64 | 102.0 | 22 | 2,654 | 974 |
| 96 | 96 | 84.6 | 26 | 3,356 | 1,022 |
| 128 | 128 | 76.4 | 30 | 3,905 | 1,074 |
| 192 | 192 | 69.0 | 37 | 4,601 | 1,143 |
| 256 | 256 | 63.5 | 44 | 5,155 | 1,178 |
| 384 | 340 | 64.6 | 55 | 5,071 | 1,180 |

From 452 to 63.5 Wh/M. 7.1× on the same model, the same two cards, the same prompts. The power draw rises by about a third, 39 percent: 850 W at the top of the table, 1,178 W at the best row. What moves far more is how many tokens that power produces, from 522 a second to 5,155, 9.9×. Median latency goes from 15 ms to 44 ms, which no user will notice. Past that row the curve turns: at a cap of 384 the same cards read 64.6 Wh/M at 55 ms.

See, this is the part the invoice hides. A GPU is a bus. The diesel per trip goes up a little when the bus is full; the diesel per passenger comes down a long way. An enterprise assistant that serves a handful of people at a time is the bus running nearly empty, and in the deployments I see it is the usual case.

The same ladder for a small model on one card: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on 1 × H100 goes from 126 Wh/M at a running batch of 8 to 19.5 at 511, a 6.5× drop, while its power rises 41 percent. All eleven of its configurations are on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#concurrency).

## What that does to the bill, and to the carbon

Electricity first, because people always ask and the answer is small. 63.5 Wh per million tokens is 63.5 kWh per billion. At USD 0.10 per kWh, my assumption and not a source figure, a billion tokens is USD 6.35 of electricity, or 0.6 cents per million. Nobody will change a decision over that. The number matters because it tracks GPU-hours, and GPU-hours are where the money actually goes. Halve the watt-hours per token and you have halved the GPU time per token, on the same kit.

Carbon depends on where the socket is. Multiply Wh/M by the grid's grams of CO2e per kWh and divide by a thousand, and you get kilograms per billion tokens. On Ember's 2024 annual averages the reference row is 43.7 kg per billion tokens in Saudi Arabia (689 g/kWh), 42.4 kg in Serbia (668), and 1.9 kg in Norway (30). Same tokens, same cards, 23× apart. Location moves the carbon and does nothing to the energy, which is why the two should never be reported as one number.

## What I am not telling you

Closed-weight models served over an API. The leaderboard cannot measure them, and neither can anyone outside those companies, so I say nothing about them. Sliced GPUs: NVIDIA does not publish power per MIG slice and no public benchmark has measured one, which is the first gap we will fill with a measurement of our own, on our own rig, with the protocol and the logs published. And the lightly loaded reality: every row on the index is the best case under a latency limit. Your deployment sits above it. The concurrency table tells you how far.

I wish I could tell you the platform we build already measures this for every tenant. It does not, yet. When it does, it will be published here under the same review as any other row, labelled as ours, beside the public ones.

## What to do with it

Ask your vendor for Wh per million output tokens at your concurrency, not theirs. Measure your own with DCGM; one row is an afternoon's work on a card you control, and a MIG pair is an evening. And put the number in the RFP. The clause is on the [why page](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/). If two bidders give you the same figure at the same load, you have learned something. If neither can, you have learned more.

*References*

Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. # The energy behind the token

> Lead Green is a public index of LLM inference energy per token: GPU watt-hours per million output tokens by model and GPU, with grid carbon and open API.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

Lead Green is a public index of **LLM inference energy per token**: the GPU watt-hours it takes to serve a million output tokens, by model, GPU and configuration, with the grid carbon to price it anywhere. Every figure is from a named public measurement or a manufacturer's specification, dated and linked. The data is open, there is a JSON API and an MCP server, and anyone with a GPU will be able to add a measurement.

**Unit** watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M). One Wh/M is 0.0036 joules per token. GPU only, busy server. Every row is a floor. Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Lead Green: the energy behind the token. https://leadgreen.ai/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.  [Read the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/) [Why it matters](https://leadgreen.ai/why/) [Use the data](https://leadgreen.ai/api/)
-  **Lowest floor on the index:**  13.0 Wh/M  Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 1 × B200. Running batch 2,043, median ITL 125 ms.
-  **Reference floor:**  63.5 Wh/M  Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100. Running batch 256, median ITL 44 ms. The carbon table is priced on this row.
-  **Highest floor on the index:**  572.9 Wh/M  Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8, 8 × H100. Running batch 255, median ITL 67 ms.

A million output tokens is roughly three quarters of a million words of English. The index spans **44×** from its lowest row to its highest, and the same model on the same two GPUs moves **7.1×** depending on how busy the server is. Every row is a floor. The number a buyer should ask for is the one measured on their own server.

*What it is*

## One unit, one place, for people and for machines  Index

*Why it exists*

## Everyone buys tokens. Nobody is told the energy.

Enterprises are buying GPUs by the rack and tokens by the billion, and neither invoice carries an energy figure. Model vendors have published, at most, a per-prompt average of energy, carbon and water with no load, output length or method a buyer could compare ([Google, August 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15734); [Mistral, July 2025](https://mistral.ai/news/our-contribution-to-a-global-environmental-standard-for-ai)). None publishes watt-hours per million output tokens at a stated concurrency. The cloud providers do not itemise one. The measurements that do exist are academic and scattered across leaderboards and papers, in different units, on different hardware, under different load. A CIO who wants to know what a million tokens costs in watt-hours has nowhere to look it up.

Meanwhile the questions are arriving. Boards want the AI line in the energy report. Auditors want to know how Scope 2, or Scope 3 for a hosted API, grows when the assistants roll out. The EU AI Act already requires providers of general-purpose AI models to document the model's energy consumption for the AI Office, with exemptions for open-weight models. No law asks anyone for serving energy per token; buyers should. Sovereign and on-premise deployments run inside a fixed power envelope, so energy per token sets how much AI a site can serve at all.

Lead Green puts the public measurements in one unit on one page, explains what they mean, exposes them to software, and adds measurements of its own as they are made. It is run and paid for by [Katonic](https://www.katonic.ai), which sells a sovereign AI platform and benefits when buyers ask the questions on this site. It takes no money from hardware, cloud or model vendors.

*Why you should care*

At the reference row, per megawatt-hour of GPU energy. At the top of the concurrency ladder the same megawatt-hour serves 2.2 billion. On a fixed feed, the number decides how much AI you can run. Location23× carbon, same tokens

Saudi grid against Norwegian grid, 2024 averages. Geography changes the carbon number and not the energy number. [One page per grid.](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) ReportingE1-5 ESRS

European sustainability reporting asks for energy consumption in MWh. AI served on your own GPUs is a growing line inside it, and it needs a per-token figure to forecast. RegulationAnnex XI 1.2(e) EU AI Act

Providers of general-purpose AI models must record the model's known or estimated energy consumption in documentation held for the AI Office. The law's figure is training energy in MWh, and it does not reach buyers. No law yet asks anyone for serving energy per token. This index is the figure buyers need while that stays true. Cheap, and that is the point0.6¢ per million tokens

Electricity at the reference row, priced at USD 0.10 per kWh, at the floor; a lightly loaded server pays several times this. Trivial as a bill, decisive as a signal: it tracks GPU-hours, which is where the real money goes.

*Who it is for*

## Five desks, one number

### CIO and CTO

To size a GPU estate against a power budget, to know what on-premise inference would cost in energy before a hosted invoice becomes a power bill, and to answer the board. Hosted APIs cannot be measured from outside; [the why page](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) says what to ask the vendor instead.

### Sustainability officer

To put AI serving into the energy and Scope 2 lines with a defensible method, and to know which questions to send back to the vendor.

### Platform engineer

To see what concurrency, quantisation and GPU generation do to energy per token, and to measure their own cluster against a public baseline.

### Procurement

To ask every bidder for the same figure at the same load, in [a clause](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/) that names the unit and the latency limit and tells you what to fill in, with a scoring method beside it.

### Facility and capacity planner

You own the feed, the power envelope and the capacity meeting. The index gives you GPU energy per unit of work and the two multipliers that take it to the meter, so a contracted feed becomes tokens per hour at a stated PUE and server overhead. It does not give you PUE, water, waste heat or anything else in facility units.

*How to use it*

## Three ways in

1. **Read.** Start with the three tiles and the concurrency section of [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/). If you take one thing away, take the 7.1× ladder.
2. **Compute.** Pull `index.json` and `grid.json` from the [API](https://leadgreen.ai/api/). Multiply Wh per million by your monthly tokens for energy; multiply by your grid's gCO2e per kWh and divide by 1,000 for kg CO2e per billion tokens.
3. **Ask.** Add the [MCP server](https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/) to your assistant and ask in plain words. It answers with the row, the source and the caveat.

Latest from the blog: [How much energy does an AI query use?](https://leadgreen.ai/blog/how-much-energy-does-an-ai-query-use/).

## Asked about Lead Green

### What is Lead Green?

A public index of LLM inference energy per token: the GPU watt-hours it takes to serve a million output tokens, by model, GPU and configuration, with the grid carbon to price it anywhere. Every figure is from a named public measurement or a manufacturer's specification, dated and linked. The data is open under CC BY 4.0, there is a JSON API and an MCP server, and it is a Katonic project.

### What unit does the index use?

Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M); one Wh/M is 0.0036 joules per token. The index runs from 13.0 Wh/M (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 1 × B200) to 572.9 Wh/M (Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8, 8 × H100), GPU only, measured on a busy server; every row is a floor that a real deployment sits above.

### Where do the figures come from?

Energy per token from the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026, retrieved 26 September 2026); grid carbon intensity from Ember's yearly electricity data (October 2026 release, 2024); GPU power ceilings from NVIDIA's published specifications; per-query energy from the AI Energy Score's December 2025 round. Every source is listed with its version, licence and retrieval date in the index's ledger.

### Is the data open, and how do I get it?

Yes. The compilation and site text are CC BY 4.0 and the sources keep their own licences. Every table is static JSON under https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ with CORS open and no key, there is an MCP server for AI assistants, every page has a Markdown copy at its URL followed by index.md, and llms.txt at the site root lists all of it.

### Who runs and pays for Lead Green?

Lead Green is run and paid for by Katonic, which sells a sovereign AI platform and benefits when buyers ask the questions on this site. It takes no money from hardware, cloud or model vendors. The publisher is Katonic AI Technology Ltd, registered in the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC), United Arab Emirates; the editor is Prem Naraindas.
