# Nine reasons to know your watt-hours per million tokens

> Why GPU energy per million output tokens belongs in procurement, operations and reporting, with the working, the sources and what to do on Monday.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/why/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/why/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Why it matters*

The number is small, cheap to buy and easy to ignore. It is also the only figure that ties a model, a GPU and a workload to a power feed, a carbon line and a utilisation rate at the same time. Here is why each of those matters, with the working shown.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Why it matters. https://leadgreen.ai/why/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [1 Utilisation](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#utilisation)
- [2 Power](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#power)
- [3 The board](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#board)
- [4 The regulator](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#regulator)
- [5 Location](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#location)
- [6 The SCI](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#sci)
- [7 Cheap](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#cheap)
- [8 Sliced GPUs](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#mig)
- [9 Monday](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#monday)
- [Hosted API](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#faq)

*1*

## It is a utilisation meter

Take one model on one pair of GPUs and change nothing but how many requests the server holds at once. On the index, Qwen 3 32B on two H100 cards goes from **452 Wh/M** at a running batch of 8 to **63.5 Wh/M** at 256. That is 7.1× on the same hardware. The cards' draw rises 39 percent, from 850 W to 1,178 W, while the tokens they produce each second rise 9.9×, and median inter-token latency stays at 44 ms or under.

Read it the other way round. A high energy per token does not mean the GPU is working hard. It means the GPU is drawing close to full power and producing few tokens, which is what an under-used server looks like from the wall socket. Energy per token is the utilisation rate expressed in a unit finance can see. If yours is high, you are paying for silicon that is waiting.

Source: [ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/), Text Conversation, all nine measured configurations of Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100. Full ladder on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#concurrency).

*2*

## Power is the ceiling

A data hall, a sovereign site or a telco exchange has a fixed power envelope long before it has a fixed GPU count. Energy per token converts that envelope into capacity. One megawatt-hour of GPU energy serves **15.8 billion output tokens** at the reference row (63.5 Wh/M). At the top of the concurrency ladder, 452 Wh/M, the same megawatt-hour serves **2.2 billion**.

An eight-GPU DGX B200 is rated at about 14.3 kW, and each B200 can be configured up to 1,000 W. Those are the numbers a facility engineer works with. What they buy depends entirely on the Wh/M the platform achieves, which is why the figure belongs in the capacity plan and not only in the sustainability report. To take a GPU figure to the facility meter, multiply by the system-to-GPU power ratio and the site's PUE; the [method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method) works one example.

Sources: [ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) for the rows; [NVIDIA DGX B200 product page](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/dgx-b200/) and the [HGX B200 product carbon footprint summary](https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/documents/HGX-B200-PCF-Summary.pdf) (July 2025) for the ceilings.

*3*

## The board will ask

Under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, disclosure E1-5 asks for total energy consumption in MWh from own operations, split by fossil, nuclear and renewable sources. AI served on GPUs the company runs is a new and growing line inside that total, and its electricity lands in Scope 2. Tokens bought from a hosted API are different: that electricity is the provider's Scope 2 and the buyer's Scope 3 category 1 (purchased goods and services), and it sits outside the buyer's E1-5 MWh. A company that cannot say how many MWh its assistants used last quarter, or how many they will use next year as adoption grows, cannot fill in the line with a method it can defend.

Energy per million tokens is the forecasting unit in both cases. Tokens served next year multiplied by Wh/M gives the MWh. Without the first factor the second is a guess.

Sources: [Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2023/2772/oj), ESRS E1-5 "Energy consumption and mix", paragraph 37 (energy consumption related to own operations), carried into ESRS (2026) for financial years from 2027, and E1-6 (Scope 2, location-based and market-based); GHG Protocol Scope 3, category 1, purchased goods and services.

Regulatory summaries on this site are as at 27 September 2026, for orientation, and are not legal advice.

*4*

## What the regulator asks, and what it does not

The EU AI Act ([Regulation (EU) 2024/1689](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)) requires providers of general-purpose AI models to keep technical documentation, and Annex XI lists what it must contain. Section 1, point 2(e) names the "known or estimated energy consumption of the model", and adds that where it is unknown it may be based on the computational resources used. The duty sits with the model provider, not with the company deploying the model.

Two limits apply. Article 53(2) lifts this duty from models released under a free and open-source licence with public weights, unless the model carries systemic risk. Every model on this index is open-weight, though whether each licence and model qualifies is for its provider to show. Article 111(3) gives models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 until 2 August 2027 to comply. So for many rows on this index no energy documentation is yet required by law.

That documentation stays between the provider and the AI Office. Annex XII, the information a provider must give downstream, has no energy item, and the Code of Practice's Model Documentation Form marks its energy fields for the AI Office and national authorities only, asks for training energy in megawatt-hours, and records inference as compute in floating-point operations. So the Act does not put a serving energy figure in a buyer's hands. Lead Green expects buyers to ask for one anyway, at their own load, and the index is the public baseline for that question.

The reporting duty that reaches a data centre operator is not the AI Act. Under the Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791, Article 12, and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364, a data centre with an installed IT power demand of at least 500 kW reports to the European database, first by 15 September 2024 and then by 15 May every year. Annex II sets the indicators: total energy consumption, IT equipment energy, PUE, water use, renewable share and waste heat reuse. None of them can be filled from this index, because they are facility figures. Wh/M sits one level beneath the IT energy line: it is how that total divides across tenants and workloads, and why two tenants on identical racks can draw the same kilowatts and serve very different token volumes. The AI Act, by contrast, asks nothing of an operator serving models to tenants unless the operator becomes a provider by modifying a model with more than about a third of its original training compute (Commission guidelines, July 2025).

Source: [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), Article 53(1)(a) and (2), Article 111(3), Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(e), and Annex XII; General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, Model Documentation Form. [Directive (EU) 2023/1791](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2023/1791/oj), Article 12 and Annex VII; [Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg_del/2024/1364/oj), Articles 1 and 3 and Annex II; Commission guidelines on general-purpose AI models, July 2025.

Legal texts are summarised as at 27 September 2026 for orientation and are not legal advice. ESRS (2026), adopted 3 July 2026, keeps E1-5 and applies to financial years from 1 January 2027. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026, moved the high-risk dates to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 and left the general-purpose model duties unchanged.

*5*

## Location changes carbon 23×, and not energy

Energy per token is a property of the model, the hardware and the load. Carbon per token adds the grid. On Ember's 2024 annual averages, Saudi Arabia's grid runs at 689 gCO2e per kWh and Norway's at 30. The reference row priced against them gives **43.7 kg CO2e per billion tokens** in one place and **1.9 kg** in the other, for identical tokens on identical GPUs.

So a sovereign or in-country deployment changes the carbon figure with no change to the energy figure, in either direction. Which is why the two numbers should be reported separately, and why a claim about one should never be dressed as a claim about the other.

Source: [Ember, Yearly electricity data](https://ember-energy.org/data/yearly-electricity-data/), October 2026 release, emissions intensity of total generation, 2024: a lifecycle, generation-based figure for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file. 193 countries in [the API](https://leadgreen.ai/api/); 22 on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#carbon).

*6*

## It is the E in the SCI

ISO/IEC 21031:2024 standardises the Software Carbon Intensity specification: SCI = ((E × I) + M) per R, where E is the energy consumed by the software, I the carbon intensity of that energy, M the embodied emissions of the hardware, and R the functional unit. For a language model, R is naturally a million output tokens. E is the energy of all the hardware reserved for the service; this index supplies the GPU part of it, which is a floor. I is the location-based grid intensity, which Ember supplies. M is an amortised share of the embodied emissions, not a total: TE × (TiR / EL) × (RR / ToR).

NVIDIA's 2,274 kg CO2e cradle-to-gate figure for an eight-GPU HGX B200 baseboard covers the baseboard only; it excludes the host, the use phase and end of life. As an illustration, spread over 5 years of continuous use it comes to 51.9 g an hour. DeepSeek V3.1 on 8 × B200 serves 32.5 million output tokens an hour at its index row, so M is about 1.6 g per million tokens, against E × I of 5.0 g on the Norwegian grid. The 5-year life is an assumption for the illustration, not a source figure.

Anyone building an SCI score for an AI service needs the E. The index is a public place to get a baseline for its GPU part.

Sources: [ISO/IEC 21031:2024](https://www.iso.org/standard/86612.html), Information technology, Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) specification; [NVIDIA, Product Carbon Footprint Summary for HGX B200](https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/documents/HGX-B200-PCF-Summary.pdf), July 2025.

*7*

## Electricity per token is cheap. That is exactly why the number matters.

At the reference row, a million output tokens takes 63.5 Wh, which at USD 0.10 per kWh is **0.6 US cents**. A billion tokens is about USD 6.35. Nobody will make a decision on that bill.

But the bill is not the point. Energy per token is the power a GPU draws multiplied by the time it spends on the tokens. Watt-hours per token track GPU-hours per token, and GPU-hours are the real cost of serving, whether they are rented at cloud rates or depreciated on a balance sheet. A configuration that halves Wh/M has halved the GPU-hours per token. The electricity figure is a cheap instrument to put on an expensive thing.

Working: 63.5 Wh per million tokens is 63.5 kWh per billion; at USD 0.10 per kWh that is USD 6.35 per billion tokens, or 0.6 cents per million. The electricity price is an assumption for the worked example, not a source figure.

*8*

## Sliced GPUs are unmeasured

Multi-Instance GPU lets one A100, H100, H200 or B200 be split into up to seven isolated slices, and it is how many enterprise and telco platforms serve several small models from one card. NVIDIA publishes the slice shapes. It does not publish power draw per slice, and neither of the two public benchmarks on the index has measured a sliced card. So the configuration a great many production deployments actually run in has no public energy figure at all.

That is the first gap Lead Green intends to close with measurements of its own. First, Qwen 3 14B in BF16 on one H100, the whole card against two 3g.40gb slices each serving its own BF16 copy under the same load, beside the public 1 × H100 rows for the same model. Second, Qwen 3 32B, the whole card in BF16 against two 3g.40gb slices each serving an FP8 or INT4 copy, labelled as not like-for-like on precision. GPU power is sampled through NVIDIA DCGM, with hardware, driver, engine and prompt set named. A 32B model in BF16 does not fit a 3g.40gb slice, which is why the like-for-like run is the 14B. Until it is published, Lead Green's working answer for a sliced deployment is "unknown, and in our view above the index".

Source: [NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU User Guide, supported MIG profiles](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/tesla/mig-user-guide/supported-mig-profiles.html), last updated 11 September 2026. Profiles on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#hardware).

*9*

## What to do on Monday

1. **Ask the vendor for Wh per million output tokens at your concurrency.** Not at theirs. Name the model, the precision, the GPU count, the workload and the latency limit, and ask for the average running batch the figure was measured at (the number of requests the server was decoding at once, not the queue). Workload matters as much as load: on the same leaderboard, the Problem Solving task costs 3 to 41 times the energy per response of Text Conversation for the same model on the same GPU, because its answers run 5,361 to 8,969 tokens against 462 to 1,464, and because the long outputs cut the batch the server can hold, so energy per token itself is 2.2 to 3.3 times the Text Conversation figure for the Qwen and DeepSeek pairs, and 0.7 to 1.0 times it for the four Nemotron pairs. If the vendor cannot answer, the index gives you the floor to hold them to. If you buy tokens from a hosted API rather than run GPUs, the concurrency is the provider's, not yours: send the questions in the [hosted API section](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) instead.
2. **Measure your own.** NVIDIA DCGM reports the GPU's energy counter; read it at the start and end of a steady load, divide the energy by the output tokens served, and you have your own row. The [measurement protocol](https://leadgreen.ai/contribute/#protocol) is short and the result can be listed beside the public ones.
3. **Put the number in the RFP.** One clause, below, turns a marketing conversation into a comparable figure across every bidder.

Source for the workload comparison: ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0, Problem Solving (gpqa) against Text Conversation, energy-optimal rows at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default for both tasks; no measured configuration exceeds 326 ms, so the limit changes no row; 11 model and GPU pairs measured on both.

*The clause and the scoring method*

Both have their own page, with a variant for hosted APIs: [How to put AI energy efficiency in an RFP](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/). Fill [N] with the running batch you expect in production and [T] and [T99] with the latency your users will accept, and use the same values for every bidder.

*Hosted API*

## If you buy tokens from a hosted API

The index cannot measure a hosted API. The benchmark behind it serves open-weight models on GPUs it controls, at a load it sets. A hosted provider's fleet is closed to outsiders, its batches mix every customer's traffic, and it states no concurrency, so there is no configuration to measure and no row to compare, and "at your concurrency" has no meaning. What a buyer can do is ask the provider in writing for the figures below, then use the index to judge whether the first answer is plausible.

The reporting line differs too. On GPUs you run, the electricity is your own consumption: it goes into your ESRS E1-5 energy total, and its emissions into your Scope 2. When you buy tokens from a hosted API, the same electricity is part of the provider's operations: it is the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3 category 1 (purchased goods and services), and it sits outside your E1-5 total. Wh/M is the forecasting unit in both cases. Only the line it lands on differs.

**Ask the provider, in writing:**

1. The fleet-average GPU energy per million output tokens for the model and tier you buy, at the fleet's real utilisation over the period and not a best case, with the boundary stated: GPU only, or with host, network and cooling included.
2. The regions that serve your traffic, and the grid or contracted supply behind each.
3. The power usage effectiveness (PUE) of those sites, and the host-to-GPU power ratio of the serving systems.
4. The carbon factor: its source, its year, whether it is combustion-only or lifecycle, and any market-based instruments netted off, stated separately from the location-based figure.
5. The rule that allocates a shared fleet's energy to your account.
6. A restatement of these figures every quarter for the term of the contract.
7. For any per-prompt figure the provider publishes, the output length, the concurrency and the boundary behind it.

Together they give the supplier-specific figure your Scope 3 category 1 line needs, and the index tells you whether the first number is plausible.

The clause for a hosted or shared inference service is on [the RFP page](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#hosted), as the second lot beside the on-premise clause; the cannot-measure and confidential rules apply to it too.

*Questions*

## Asked about why the number matters

### Does the EU AI Act require reporting the energy used by AI inference?

Not per inference. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers of general-purpose AI models to keep technical documentation for the AI Office, and Annex XI, section 1, point 2(e) names the model's known or estimated energy consumption: a training figure in MWh, held by the provider, which does not reach buyers. Article 53(2) lifts the duty from models released under a free and open-source licence with public weights unless they carry systemic risk, and Article 111(3) gives models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 until 2 August 2027. No law asks anyone for serving energy per token. Regulatory summaries on this site are as at 27 September 2026, for orientation, and are not legal advice.

### Which line of ESRS E1 does AI inference energy go on?

For GPUs you run, the electricity is energy consumption from own operations under ESRS E1-5 (paragraph 37) and its emissions are Scope 2 under E1-6, location-based and market-based. Tokens bought from a hosted API are the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3, category 1, purchased goods and services. In both cases the forecasting unit is energy per million tokens: tokens served next year multiplied by Wh/M gives the MWh.

### Why does an idle GPU use more energy per token than a busy one?

Because the cards' power does not fall in step with their work. On the index, Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 goes from 452 Wh/M at a running batch of 8 to 63.5 Wh/M at 256, 7.1× on the same hardware, while the cards' draw rises only 39 percent. A high energy per token is what an under-used server looks like from the wall socket: you are paying for silicon that is waiting.

### Does where I run AI change its energy per token?

No; it changes the carbon. The same tokens on the same GPUs use the same energy anywhere. On Ember's 2024 figures the reference row carries 43.7 kg CO2e per billion tokens on Saudi Arabia's grid (689 gCO2e per kWh) and 1.9 kg on Norway's (30), 23× apart.

### Is the electricity for AI inference expensive?

No, and that is the point. At the reference row and USD 0.10 per kWh the electricity costs about 0.6 cents per million tokens at the floor; a lightly loaded server pays several times that. Trivial as a bill, decisive as a signal: energy per token tracks GPU-hours, which is where the real money goes.

Every question on the site, with a link to the page that answers it, is on [the questions page](https://leadgreen.ai/faq/); the terms are defined in [the glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/).

---

# How to put AI energy efficiency in an RFP

> The clause to paste, the scoring box and a hosted-API variant: GPU watt-hours per million output tokens at a stated running batch and latency.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Why it matters](https://leadgreen.ai/why/) · Procurement*

Ask every bidder for the same figure at the same load: GPU energy per million output tokens (Wh/M) for each proposed model and serving configuration, measured at steady state on the proposed hardware at a stated average running batch, with median and p99 inter-token latency reported, GPU energy only, naming the method, the tool, the versions and the date. Score the answers with a gate on completeness, a floor from [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/)'s rows for the same model and GPU, a challenge at 10 percent below the floor, and the consistency check Wh/M = average GPU power ÷ output tokens per second × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600. The clause, the scoring box and a second clause for hosted APIs are below, ready to paste.

**Unit** watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M), GPU only. **Floors** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json) and [models.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/models.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. How to put AI energy efficiency in an RFP. https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [What to ask for](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#ask)
- [The clause](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#clause)
- [Scoring](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#scoring)
- [Hosted API](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#hosted)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#sources)

*What to ask for*

## Six things every answer must carry

An energy figure without its load, its latency and its boundary cannot be compared with another bidder's. The clause asks for all six together; the scoring box treats an answer missing any of them as not stated.

*The figures the clause asks every bidder for, and why each is there*

| Ask for | Unit | Why it is in the clause |
|---|---|---|
| GPU energy per million output tokens | Wh/M | The comparable figure. One Wh/M is 0.0036 joules per output token; the index runs from 13.0 to 572.9 Wh/M across its rows. |
| Average running batch held, and the cap | requests | Load moves the figure more than hardware does: 7.1× for the reference model on the same cards between a running batch of 8 and 256. A cap of 256 with eight users is a running batch of eight. |
| Median and p99 inter-token latency | ms | The same latency limit for every bidder is what makes two figures comparable; a looser limit buys a lower number. |
| Output tokens per second and average GPU power | tokens/s, W | The consistency check: Wh/M must equal power ÷ throughput × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600. On the reference row, 1,177.9 W ÷ 5,155.5 tokens per second = 63.47 Wh/M. |
| The boundary statement | GPU only | So that no bidder folds host, network or cooling into the figure, or leaves them out without saying so. Facility multipliers are the operator's own and belong in a separate line. |
| Method, tool, versions, date, prompt set | text | What makes the measurement repeatable and the floor comparison fair; the [measurement protocol](https://leadgreen.ai/contribute/#protocol) names the defaults. |

Power usage effectiveness and renewable share describe the building, not the work. Keep them in the facility section of the RFP; the clause below measures the model, the GPUs and the load.

*The clause*

## On-premise or dedicated GPUs, ready to paste

*RFP clause, ready to paste*

"The bidder shall state the GPU energy per million output tokens (Wh/M) for each proposed model and serving configuration, measured at steady state with the proposed serving engine on the proposed hardware, at an average running batch of [N] and with median inter-token latency not exceeding [T] ms and p99 inter-token latency not exceeding [T99] ms, both reported, on the prompt set supplied by the buyer in Annex [X], stating the average prompt and output token counts measured; where the buyer supplies none, on the LM Arena conversation sample used by the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0, named as such. Steady state, running batch and latency are as defined in the Lead Green measurement protocol v0.2 (leadgreen.ai/contribute/#protocol): a fixed cap of [N] sequences, held at least five minutes after warm-up and for at least 1,000 requests; the bidder shall report both the cap and the average running batch the server actually held, and the median and p99 inter-token latency over the same window. The bidder shall name the measurement method, the sampling tool, the software versions and the date. The figure shall be GPU energy only; host, network and cooling energy, where measured, shall be reported as separate figures and not folded in. The bidder shall attach the GPU power log and serving-engine log from which the figure was computed and shall state time to first token at the same load. The buyer may repeat the measurement on the delivered system at acceptance with the same prompt set; a result more than [X] percent above the stated figure is a non-conformance. Figures for sliced (MIG) configurations shall be measured with every slice on the card serving the proposed workload at the same time, reporting the card's energy per million output tokens, the slice profile, the slice count and the slices loaded. No figure may divide the card's energy by a slice count or come from a run in which any slice sat idle. A figure derived from a whole-card measurement at a different profile is not acceptable. Any carbon figure quoted shall name the grid, the emission factor source and year, whether the factor is combustion-only or lifecycle, and whether any market-based instruments have been applied, with the location-based figure stated in all cases. A bidder that cannot measure GPU energy for the proposed service, for example a hosted API on a closed-weight model, shall state that it cannot, shall attach the model provider's published energy documentation if any (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(e)), and shall not substitute a per-query or per-request figure that lacks the output token count, the concurrency and the hardware. A figure withheld as confidential is treated as not stated. The bidder may mark the raw logs confidential; the figure, the method, the running batch, the latency and the inclusion statement are not confidential and will be shared across the evaluation panel."

Fill [N] with the running batch you expect in production and [T] and [T99] with the latency your users will accept. The index uses 500 ms, the leaderboard's default, as a benchmark ceiling, not a recommendation, and no measured configuration reaches it. For an interactive assistant set [T] where your users would notice, and use the same [N] and [T] for every bidder. Everything else in the clause is there so that two bidders' numbers can be compared.

*Scoring*

## How to score the answers

Seven rules, in order. The floor comes from the index's rows for the same model and GPU, so a bidder's number is checked against a public measurement rather than against the other bidders.

*Scoring the answers*

1. **Gate.** An answer counts only if it carries the figure, the cap and the average running batch held, median and p99 inter-token latency, average output tokens per response, output tokens per second, average GPU power summed across cards, the method, the tool, the versions, the date and the GPU-only statement. An answer missing any of them scores zero on this criterion and is not disqualified.
2. **Floor.** For the same model and GPU, the floor is the configuration in `models/<slug>.json` with the smallest average running batch at or above [N] whose median inter-token latency is at or under [T] ms; if there is none, the configuration with the highest measured running batch.
3. **Tolerance.** An answer more than 10 percent below the floor is challenged, and the bidder supplies the raw power and engine logs. The protocol's own repeat threshold is 5 percent.
4. **Consistency.** Wh/M must equal average GPU power ÷ output tokens per second × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600. On the reference row: 1,177.9 W ÷ 5,155.5 tokens per second × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600 = 63.47 Wh/M. An answer that fails the check beyond rounding is treated as not stated.
5. **Cannot measure.** An answer that declares it cannot measure, as the clause provides, is scored as not stated, not compared.
6. **Confidential.** A figure withheld as confidential is scored as not stated. Logs may be confidential; the figure, method, running batch, latency and inclusion statement may not.
7. **Where Katonic bids.** Lead Green is a Katonic project. In a tender where Katonic may bid, take floor values from the ML.ENERGY rows directly and disclose the compilation, using the wording in [Using the index in a tender](https://leadgreen.ai/about/#tender).

*Hosted API*

## If the lot is a hosted or shared inference service

The index cannot measure a hosted API: its fleet is closed, its batches mix every customer's traffic and it states no concurrency. The clause below asks the provider for the fleet-average figure and the facts behind it, and the index tells the buyer whether the first answer is plausible. The [why page](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) has the seven questions to ask in writing and the reporting line the tokens land on.

*RFP clause, hosted or shared inference service*

"For a hosted or shared inference service, the bidder shall state, for each proposed model and service tier, the fleet-average GPU energy per million output tokens (Wh/M) over the preceding quarter at the fleet's actual utilisation, and shall state whether host, network and cooling energy are included; where they are measured they shall be reported as separate figures and not folded in. The bidder shall name the facilities and grid regions that will serve the buyer's traffic and the grid or contracted supply behind each, shall state their power usage effectiveness and the host-to-GPU power ratio of the serving systems, and shall state the rule by which the energy of a shared fleet is allocated to the buyer. Any carbon figure quoted shall name the grid, the emission factor source and year, whether the factor is combustion-only or lifecycle, and whether any market-based instruments have been applied, with the location-based figure stated in all cases. Any per-prompt or per-request figure offered shall state the output length, the concurrency and the boundary behind it. The bidder shall restate these figures to the buyer every quarter for the term of the contract. A bidder that cannot state the fleet figure shall say so; that answer is scored as not stated, not compared."

Use it as the second lot beside the on-premise clause above, so a tender with both lots scores both. The cannot-measure and confidential rules in "Scoring the answers" apply to it too.

*Sources*

## Where the floors come from

[ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371). The floor for a model and GPU is the configuration in `models/<slug>.json` that the scoring box names; the tolerance and repeat thresholds are the index's own (10 and 5 percent).

**Cite as.** Lead Green, a Katonic project. Green Tokens: GPU energy per million output tokens. https://leadgreen.ai/index/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. © 2026 Katonic AI Technology Ltd. Licensed [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), offered as-is and without warranty; state whether you changed any rows or columns. Underlying data: ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (The ML.ENERGY Initiative; Apache 2.0 per the ml-energy/benchmark-v3 dataset card; cite Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks, arXiv 2505.06371); Ember, Yearly electricity data, October 2026 release (CC BY 4.0); AI Energy Score (Apache-2.0 as tagged on its Space; results reproduced as facts with attribution); NVIDIA figures reproduced as facts from the documents named in the sources ledger.

*Questions*

## Asked about AI energy in an RFP

### How do I put AI energy efficiency in an RFP?

Ask every bidder for the same figure at the same load: GPU energy per million output tokens (Wh/M) for each proposed model and serving configuration, measured at steady state on the proposed hardware at a stated average running batch, with median and p99 inter-token latency reported, on the buyer's prompt set or the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's conversation sample, GPU energy only, naming the method, the tool, the versions and the date. Score it with a gate on completeness, a floor from the index's rows for the same model and GPU, a challenge at 10 percent below the floor, and the consistency check Wh/M = average GPU power ÷ output tokens per second × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600. The clause and the scoring box on this page are ready to paste.

### What unit should an RFP use for AI energy?

GPU watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M), GPU energy only, at a stated running batch and latency. It is the one figure that ties a named model on named GPUs to a measured load, and it is what the index's rows are in, so every answer has a public floor to be checked against. Watt-hours per query need an output length and a load to mean anything, and power usage effectiveness describes the building, not the work.

### What running batch and latency should the RFP specify?

The running batch you expect in production, as a number [N], and the median [T] and p99 [T99] inter-token latency your users will accept, the same for every bidder. Load moves the figure more than hardware does: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 runs from 452 Wh/M at a running batch of 8 to 63.5 Wh/M at 256, 7.1× on the same cards. The index uses 500 ms as a benchmark ceiling, not a recommendation.

### How do I score a bidder's energy figure?

Gate first: an answer counts only if it carries the figure, the cap and running batch held, median and p99 latency, output tokens per response, tokens per second, average GPU power, the method, the tool, the versions, the date and the GPU-only statement. Then compare it with the floor, the index row for the same model and GPU at or above the stated running batch; challenge any answer more than 10 percent below it and ask for the power and engine logs. Last, check Wh/M = average GPU power ÷ output tokens per second × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600; an answer that fails beyond rounding is treated as not stated.

### Can I ask a hosted API provider for energy per token?

Yes, as a fleet-average figure over the preceding quarter at the fleet's actual utilisation, with the boundary stated, the serving regions and their grids named, the sites' PUE and host-to-GPU power ratio given, the rule that allocates a shared fleet's energy to your account, and a quarterly restatement for the term. The index cannot measure a hosted fleet, but it tells you whether the first answer is plausible. The electricity is the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3, category 1.

### Is PUE enough to compare AI vendors on energy?

No. Power usage effectiveness is the building's overhead on top of the IT load; it says nothing about how much work the IT load does. Two vendors at the same PUE can differ many times in GPU energy per token through model, precision, GPU generation and load. Ask for PUE in the facility section and for Wh/M at a stated load in the clause, and keep the two apart.

Every question on the site, with a link to the page that answers it, is on [the questions page](https://leadgreen.ai/faq/); the terms are defined in [the glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/).

# Green Tokens

> GPU watt-hours per million output tokens by model, GPU and configuration, from public measurements, with concurrency curves, grid carbon and sources.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/index/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/index/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*The index*

The GPU energy it takes to serve a million tokens, by model, GPU and configuration. Every figure is from a public measurement or a manufacturer's specification, and every source is listed at the foot of the page. Updated 19 October 2026.

Green here is a direction, not a verdict. This table ranks serving configurations by GPU energy per token and by nothing else.

**Unit** watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M). One Wh/M is 0.0036 joules per token. GPU only, busy server. Every row is a floor. The same data as [JSON](https://leadgreen.ai/api/) and through the [MCP server](https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/).

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Green Tokens: GPU energy per million output tokens. https://leadgreen.ai/index/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

-  **Lowest floor on the index:**  13.0 Wh/M  Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 1 × B200. Running batch 2,043, median ITL 125 ms.
-  **Reference floor:**  63.5 Wh/M  Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100. Running batch 256, median ITL 44 ms. The carbon table is priced on this row.
-  **Highest floor on the index:**  572.9 Wh/M  Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8, 8 × H100. Running batch 255, median ITL 67 ms.

A million output tokens is roughly three quarters of a million words of English. The index spans **44×** from its lowest row to its highest, and the same model on the same two GPUs moves **7.1×** depending on how busy the server is. Every row here is a floor. The number a buyer should ask for is the one measured on their own server.

*The index*

## Energy per million output tokens

32 rows, 18 open-weight models, two GPUs. Each row is the most energy-efficient configuration the ML.ENERGY benchmark found for that model on that GPU at or under a median inter-token latency of 500 ms, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, on its Text Conversation workload. No measured configuration reaches the ceiling (the highest median is 326 ms), so it selects nothing: each row is also the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at any latency. Sorted from least energy to most.

# Every table, as JSON

> The Green Tokens index as read-only JSON: index rows, per-model configurations, grid carbon, GPU hardware and per-query scores. CORS open, CC BY 4.0.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/api/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/api/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Data API*

The index is published as static JSON files under `/api/v1/`. No key, no tracking, no rate limit beyond what a static host imposes. Fetch them from a browser, a spreadsheet, a notebook or a build pipeline. Version 1 only ever adds fields; it never renames or removes them.

**Base URL** https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ · **Updated** 19 October 2026 · **Licence** CC BY 4.0 for the compilation; sources keep theirs

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Data API. https://leadgreen.ai/api/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

*Endpoints*

## 15 files  GET`/api/v1/manifest.json`
Sources, versions, retrieval dates, licences and this endpoint list. GET`/api/v1/index.json`
The index: 32 rows, one per model and GPU, energy-optimal under the latency limit, sorted ascending. GET`/api/v1/models.json`
Every model on the index with its slug, Hugging Face id, parameter counts and measured GPUs. GET`/api/v1/models/{slug}.json`
One model: every measured configuration (concurrency, parallelism, latency, power) and the best row per GPU. GET`/api/v1/grid.json`
Grid emissions intensity, gCO2e per kWh, 2024 annual average, 193 countries plus World. GET`/api/v1/hardware.json`
Manufacturer power ceilings, memory, MIG slice profiles and one embodied-carbon figure. GET`/api/v1/per-query.json`
AI Energy Score text-generation rows, December 2025 round: Wh per 1,000 queries at batch size 1 on H100 80GB GPUs (one card for classes A and B, several for C). GET`/api/v1/openapi.json`
OpenAPI 3.1 description of these endpoints. GET`/api/v1/measurements.json`
Contributed measurements accepted under the protocol, with contributor, affiliation, date, versions and MIG profile; never merged into index.json. GET`/api/v1/schema/measurement.schema.json`
JSON Schema for a contributed measurement file (protocol v0.2); the build validates every submission against it. GET`/api/v1/changes.json`
Every change to the published data or its description: date, summary, documents, reason and source version. GET`/api/v1/index.csv`
The index rows as CSV, for a spreadsheet. GET`/api/v1/types.d.ts`
TypeScript types for every document, generated from the documents. GET`/api/v1/all.zip`
Every JSON document of the current release in one zip (the same bytes as the dated release zip). GET`/api/v1/releases/index.json`
Every dated release of api/v1, each kept unchanged at releases/<date>/ with a zip of the whole release, for citation.

Model slugs are lower-case with hyphens: `deepseek-v3-1`, `gemma-3-12b`, `gemma-3-27b`, `llama-3-1-405b-instruct`, `llama-3-1-405b-instruct-fp8`, `llama-3-1-70b-instruct`, `llama-3-1-8b-instruct`, `llama-3-3-70b-instruct`, `llama-4-maverick-17b-128e-instruct-fp8`, `llama-4-scout-17b-16e-instruct`, `nvidia-nemotron-nano-12b-v2`, `nvidia-nemotron-nano-9b-v2`, `qwen-3-14b`, `qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct`, `qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-fp8`, `qwen-3-30b-a3b-instruct`, `qwen-3-32b`, `qwen-3-8b`. The list, with Hugging Face ids, is in `models.json`.

*Example*

## Fetch the index and price it on your grid

Two requests, one multiplication. Energy per million tokens times the grid's grams per kWh, divided by 1,000, is kilograms of CO2e per billion tokens.

```
curl -s https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json | jq '.rows[] | select(.slug == "qwen-3-32b")'
curl -s https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json  | jq '.areas[] | select(.iso3 == "SRB")'
```

The first returns the reference model's rows (one per GPU); the second returns Serbia at 668 gCO2e per kWh. 63.5 × 668 ÷ 1,000 = 42.4 kg CO2e per billion output tokens on the H100 row.

*From a browser*

## CORS is open

Every file under `/api/v1/` is sent with `access-control-allow-origin: *`, and a preflight `OPTIONS` request gets 204, so a page on any origin can fetch them directly.

```
const r = await fetch("https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json");
const { rows } = await r.json();
const best = rows[0];   // sorted ascending by Wh per million output tokens
console.log(best.model, best.gpu, best.wh_per_million_output_tokens);
```

### Python

```
import json, urllib.request

BASE = "https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/"
index = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(BASE + "index.json"))
grid = {a["iso3"]: a for a in json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(BASE + "grid.json"))["areas"]}

row = next(r for r in index["rows"] if r["slug"] == "qwen-3-32b" and r["gpu"] == "H100")
kg = row["wh_per_million_output_tokens"] * grid["SRB"]["g_co2e_per_kwh"] / 1000
print(row["model"], row["num_gpus"], "x", row["gpu"], round(kg, 1), "kg CO2e per billion output tokens in Serbia")
print(index["caveat"])
```

A spreadsheet can open [`index.csv`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.csv) directly. [`all.zip`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/all.zip) holds every document of the current release.

*Fields*

## What the columns mean

One table for the fields every document carries, then one per document. The build refuses to publish a field that has no description here, and [`openapi.json`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/openapi.json) and [`types.d.ts`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/types.d.ts) are generated from the same documents, so the three cannot drift apart. `joules_per_output_token` is published to seven decimals, so `wh_per_million_output_tokens` = joules × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600 holds exactly on every row.

*Fields on every document*

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| version | API major version; it changes only for a breaking change, which would ship at /api/v2/ with v1 left in place. |
| updated | Date the document was built. |
| data_version | Changes whenever a value in the document changes. Cite it with the release archive. |
| unit | Unit of the main figure in the document. |
| caveat | Carried on every document with energy figures. Please carry it into whatever you build. |
| boundary | gpu_only: GPU energy and nothing else; host, network, storage, cooling and idle time are outside it. |
| itl_deadline_ms | The median inter-token latency ceiling used to pick best rows: 500 ms, the leaderboard's default. |
| source | The source object: name, publisher, url, data_url, version, retrieval date, licence with its evidence, method, selection and citation. |
| note | How to read the document. |
| licence | Licence of the document or of its source, as stated. |

**`index.json`, 24 fields**

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| workload | The benchmark task behind the rows. |
| selection | The rule that picks each row, in words. |
| reference_row | The row the carbon table and worked examples are priced on. |
| reference_row.model | Its model. |
| reference_row.gpu | Its GPU. |
| reference_row.num_gpus | Its card count. |
| rows | One row per model and GPU, sorted ascending by Wh/M. |
| rows[].model | Display name. |
| rows[].slug | Key for models/<slug>.json. |
| rows[].model_id | Hugging Face id. |
| rows[].params_b | Total parameters, billions. |
| rows[].active_params_b | Parameters active per token, billions (they differ for mixture-of-experts models). |
| rows[].precision | Weight precision (BF16, FP8, MXFP4). |
| rows[].gpu | GPU model: H100 (H100 80GB HBM3) or B200. |
| rows[].num_gpus | Cards in the configuration. |
| rows[].wh_per_million_output_tokens | GPU energy per million output tokens, watt-hours: joules_per_output_token x 1,000,000 / 3,600, which holds exactly on every row. |
| rows[].joules_per_output_token | The source's figure, seven decimals: steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in that window (steady_state_energy_per_token). Prompt processing is included. |
| rows[].median_itl_ms | Median inter-token latency, milliseconds. |
| rows[].avg_requests_in_flight | The same value as avg_running_batch under its first name, kept in v1 and removed at v2. It is the running batch, not client-side requests outstanding. |
| rows[].gpu_power_watts_total | Average power drawn, summed across every card. |
| rows[].avg_output_tokens | Average output length per response, tokens. |
| rows[].avg_running_batch | The average number of requests the server was decoding at once over the steady-state window (vLLM num_requests_running). Queued requests are not counted. |
| rows[].max_num_seqs | The configured cap on sequences decoded at once (vLLM max_num_seqs). |
| rows[].row_id | Stable identifier, <slug>/<gpu>/<num_gpus>/<max_num_seqs>, with /r2 on a repeated run. It survives re-sorting and new rows. |

**`models.json`, 9 fields**

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| models | Every model on the index. |
| models[].slug | Model key. |
| models[].name | Display name. |
| models[].model_id | Hugging Face id. |
| models[].params_b | Total parameters, billions. |
| models[].active_params_b | Parameters active per token, billions. |
| models[].gpus | GPUs measured. |
| models[].url | URL of models/<slug>.json. |
| models[].page | URL of the model's page on the site. |

| best | The index row per GPU, keyed by GPU; each value has the configuration fields. |

| best.<key>.gpu | GPU model: H100 (H100 80GB HBM3) or B200. |
| best.<key>.num_gpus | Cards in the configuration. |

| best.<key>.precision | Weight precision (BF16, FP8, MXFP4). |
| best.<key>.max_num_seqs | The configured cap on sequences decoded at once (vLLM max_num_seqs). |
| best.<key>.avg_requests_in_flight | The same value as avg_running_batch under its first name, kept in v1 and removed at v2. It is the running batch, not client-side requests outstanding. |
| best.<key>.wh_per_million_output_tokens | GPU energy per million output tokens, watt-hours: joules_per_output_token x 1,000,000 / 3,600, which holds exactly on every row. |
| best.<key>.joules_per_output_token | The source's figure, seven decimals: steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in that window (steady_state_energy_per_token). Prompt processing is included. |
| best.<key>.median_itl_ms | Median inter-token latency, milliseconds. |
| best.<key>.p90_itl_ms | 90th percentile inter-token latency, milliseconds. |
| best.<key>.p99_itl_ms | 99th percentile inter-token latency, milliseconds. |
| best.<key>.tokens_per_second | Output throughput of the whole configuration. |
| best.<key>.gpu_power_watts_total | Average power drawn, summed across every card. |
| best.<key>.avg_output_tokens | Average output length per response, tokens. |
| best.<key>.under_itl_deadline | Whether median_itl_ms is at or under itl_deadline_ms; every published configuration currently is. |

| best.<key>.repeat | 1 for the first run of a configuration, 2 for the source's repeat of it (two Qwen 3 30B A3B configurations were run twice). |

*Versioning and licence*

## Additive only

**Caching and limits.** The files are served by GitHub Pages, which sends `Cache-Control: max-age=600`, an ETag and Last-Modified. Poll with `If-None-Match`, no more than hourly, and mirror the files rather than fetching them for each of your users: the host has a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB a month and does not allow software-as-a-service use. There is no uptime promise. The data is refreshed when a source publishes a new release, checked monthly; the date is in every document and in [`changes.json`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/changes.json).

**Version 1.** Fields are added, never renamed or removed. A new source or a re-measurement changes values, `data_version` and the `updated` date, and the change is recorded in [`changes.json`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/changes.json) and on [the index's change list](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#changes). `row_id` identifies a row across releases. A breaking change would ship as `/api/v2/` with v1 left in place.

**Licence.** The compilation, the derived figures and the site text are offered under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/): use them, credit Lead Green and the underlying source. Each source keeps its own licence, stated per source in `manifest.json` with the evidence. ML.ENERGY: The leaderboard repository the JSON comes from carries no licence file; the benchmark data is published under Apache 2.0 on the dataset card and in the NeurIPS 2025 paper, and the JSON is reproduced here as published measurements on that basis while the ML.ENERGY team is asked to confirm that the licence covers it. Ember's data is CC BY 4.0. AI Energy Score: Apache-2.0 as tagged on the Hugging Face Space; the project states no separate licence for the results file, which is reproduced as facts with attribution. NVIDIA's figures are reproduced as facts with attribution; NVIDIA grants no licence and none is claimed. The Apache License 2.0 text is in [`LICENSE`](https://leadgreen.ai/LICENSE), and `build/data/NOTICE.md` records each snapshot's source, retrieval date and terms.

**Cite as.** Lead Green, a Katonic project. Green Tokens: GPU energy per million output tokens. https://leadgreen.ai/index/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. © 2026 Katonic AI Technology Ltd. Licensed [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), offered as-is and without warranty; state whether you changed any rows or columns. Underlying data: ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (The ML.ENERGY Initiative; Apache 2.0 per the ml-energy/benchmark-v3 dataset card; cite Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks, arXiv 2505.06371); Ember, Yearly electricity data, October 2026 release (CC BY 4.0); AI Energy Score (Apache-2.0 as tagged on its Space; results reproduced as facts with attribution); NVIDIA figures reproduced as facts from the documents named in the sources ledger.

**Attribution.** If you republish the data, this line covers the CC BY 4.0 credit (it is also the `attribution` field in `manifest.json`): Green Tokens index, Lead Green, a Katonic project, https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/, CC BY 4.0. Contains data from the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (The ML.ENERGY Initiative; data compiled 2026-02-16, retrieved 2026-09-26) and Ember Yearly Electricity Data (CC BY 4.0). Changes: [none | describe].

**Releases.** Every dated release is kept unchanged at `https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/releases/<date>/` with a zip of the whole release; [`releases/index.json`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/releases/index.json) lists them with each zip's SHA-256. Cite a release, not the live files.

**OpenAPI.** A machine-readable description is at [`openapi.json`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/openapi.json), with a copy at the site root ([`/openapi.json`](https://leadgreen.ai/openapi.json)) and an RFC 9727 API catalogue at [`/.well-known/api-catalog`](https://leadgreen.ai/.well-known/api-catalog). Every change to the figures is dated on the [changes page](https://leadgreen.ai/changes/). The [MCP server](https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/) is built on these same files.

# Ask your assistant, get a sourced number

> An MCP server that gives Claude, Cursor and other assistants the Green Tokens index as tools: energy by model and GPU, estimates, carbon and sources.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*MCP server*

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets an AI assistant call tools a server exposes. Lead Green ships a small MCP server so that Claude, Cursor or any MCP-capable client can answer questions about the index with the row, the source and the caveat attached, instead of guessing.

**Package** leadgreen-mcp 0.3.1 · **Transport** stdio · **Data** the live API, with a bundled snapshot as fallback · **Licence** Apache 2.0 · **Wheel SHA-256** `54a2d0b9efdb1dd0e4cfc4619adbff38824738be2b51efca16aab9dd41faaa8b`

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. MCP server. https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

*Install*

## One line

```
pip install leadgreen-mcp
```

Or run it without installing, with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):

```
uvx leadgreen-mcp
```

The package is [leadgreen-mcp on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/leadgreen-mcp/); the source installs with `pip install "git+https://github.com/katonic-dev/leadgreen-ai#subdirectory=leadgreen-mcp"`.

The wheel itself is at `https://leadgreen.ai/dist/leadgreen_mcp-0.3.1-py3-none-any.whl` and the SHA-256 above is its hash; `pip install https://leadgreen.ai/dist/leadgreen_mcp-0.3.1-py3-none-any.whl#sha256=54a2d0b9efdb1dd0e4cfc4619adbff38824738be2b51efca16aab9dd41faaa8b` makes pip refuse a file that does not match. To rebuild it byte for byte from the site source: `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=1792454400 python -m pip wheel ./leadgreen-mcp --no-deps`. Python 3.10 or later. The server works with the `mcp` Python SDK 1.x and 2.x. It reads the API over HTTPS on first use and falls back to the snapshot bundled in the package when the site cannot be reached, so it also works offline. Every response says which it used.

*What it sends, and where*

## GET requests to one host, and nothing else

- **Where.** Only to `https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/`, or to the base you set in `LEADGREEN_API_BASE`. Plain HTTPS GET requests for the published JSON files, once per file per session.
- **What never leaves your machine.** Your questions, your token counts, your country and anything else you pass to a tool. The arithmetic happens locally.
- **No network at all.** Point `LEADGREEN_API_BASE` at a local folder holding the API files and the server makes no requests.
- **When the site cannot be reached.** After the first failed fetch the server stops trying for the rest of the session, prints one line to stderr, and answers from the snapshot bundled in the package. Every response carries `data_source` (`live`, `local folder` or `bundled snapshot`) and `data_updated`, so a session left open for a month says how old its figures are.

*Configure*

## Three clients

### Claude Desktop

Add to `claude_desktop_config.json` (Settings, Developer, Edit Config):

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "leadgreen": { "command": "leadgreen-mcp" }
  }
}
```

### Claude Code

```
claude mcp add leadgreen -- leadgreen-mcp
```

Claude Desktop started from the Finder or the Start menu may not see the folder pip installed into. If the server does not appear, use the full path that `which leadgreen-mcp` (macOS, Linux) or `where leadgreen-mcp` (Windows) prints as the command, or run `python -m leadgreen_mcp.server`.

### Cursor

Add the same block to `.cursor/mcp.json` in the project, or to the global file from Cursor Settings, MCP.

If you run it with uv rather than installing it, use `"command": "uvx", "args": ["--from", "https://leadgreen.ai/dist/leadgreen_mcp-0.3.1-py3-none-any.whl", "leadgreen-mcp"]` instead.

*Tools*

## Eight tools, one resource

*What the server exposes, and a prompt that would call it*

| Tool | Answers | Try asking |
|---|---|---|
| list_models | Every model on the index, with slugs, ids, parameter counts and measured GPUs | "Which models does Lead Green have energy figures for?" |
| energy_per_million_tokens | The index rows for one model, optionally one GPU | "What is the energy per million tokens for Llama 3.1 70B on H100?" |
| estimate | Wh and kWh for a token count, with kg CO2e for a country; optionally at a given running batch and card count, under a latency ceiling, and at the meter with your PUE and system-to-GPU power ratio | "How much energy would 50 million tokens of Qwen 3 32B use on H100s, and what is the carbon in Serbia?" |
| compare_gpus | H100 against B200 for a model, with the ratio | "How much does B200 save over H100 for DeepSeek V3.1?" |
| concurrency_curve | Energy per token at every measured concurrency | "Show me how energy per token changes with load for Qwen 3 8B on B200" |
| grid_intensity | Annual average gCO2e per kWh for a country or World, with 2023 to 2025 where Ember has them. Accepts names, ISO codes and common short forms (UK, US, Korea) | "What is the grid carbon intensity of the UK?" |
| gpu_hardware | Max TDP, memory and MIG profiles | "What MIG slices can an H200 be split into?" |
| sources | Every source, version, retrieval date, licence and endpoint | "Where do these numbers come from?" |

The resource `leadgreen://manifest` returns the same manifest as a document. Every tool response carries `caveat`, `boundary` (`gpu_only`), `data_source` and `data_updated`. The caveat is the same string the API documents carry; a well-behaved assistant repeats it.

*Worked example*

## Fifty million tokens in Serbia

The estimate tool for Qwen 3 32B on H100, 50,000,000 output tokens, country Serbia, uses the index's best H100 row (63.47 Wh/M, the API's two-decimal value) and Ember's 2024 figure for Serbia (668 gCO2e per kWh):

- Energy: 63.47 Wh/M × 50 M = **3,173.5 Wh**, or 3.1735 kWh.
- Carbon: 3.1735 kWh × 668 g ÷ 1,000 = **2.12 kg CO2e**.

Add `pue` and `system_power_ratio` and the answer also carries energy at the meter: GPU energy times the system-to-GPU power ratio times the PUE, labelled as such. Both are your figures, not the index's; the [method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method) gives the DGX B200 ratio of 1.79 as an example.

Pass `running_batch` (`requests_in_flight` is still accepted as an alias) and the tool switches from the best row to the measured configuration on the same card count nearest that running batch (pass `num_gpus` for another count; the `basis` field names the row it used), which for a lightly loaded server can multiply the answer several times. In the deployments the editor sees, that is the number that applies.

*Settings*

## Environment

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| LEADGREEN_API_BASE | Another base URL, or a local folder holding the API files. Default https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1. |
| LEADGREEN_TIMEOUT | Seconds to wait for the site before falling back to the bundled snapshot. Default 10. |

A hosted (HTTP) endpoint, so that clients need no local install, is a later step. The source is in [the repository](https://github.com/katonic-dev/leadgreen-ai).

# One number a month

> The Green Tokens newsletter: one number from the index, one note on what moved, one pointer to read further. Monthly, by email.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/newsletter/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/newsletter/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Newsletter*

The Green Tokens edition is deliberately short: **one number** from the index, **one note** on what moved it or what it means, and **one pointer** to something worth reading. If the index did not change, the note says so. No round-ups, no sponsors.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Newsletter. https://leadgreen.ai/newsletter/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

*Subscribe*

## Email edition

The email edition is being set up. Until it opens, the meter runs inside [Own Your AI](https://www.linkedin.com/newsletters/own-your-ai-7508174547041292288/), the fortnightly LinkedIn newsletter, which will carry one number from this index in every issue from its next edition.[Read Own Your AI on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/newsletters/own-your-ai-7508174547041292288/)[Blog RSS feed](https://leadgreen.ai/feed.xml)

*Format*

## What an edition looks like

*Sample, built from the current index*

**The number.** 63.5 Wh per million output tokens: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, the index's reference row, at a running batch of 256 and 44 ms median inter-token latency.

**The note.** The same model on the same cards reads 452 Wh/M at a running batch of 8. The 7.1× between those two rows is not the model and not the hardware. It is how busy the server was.

**The pointer.** ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0, Text Conversation tab, sorted by energy per token, with the About tab open beside it for the method.

**Cadence.** Monthly, on the first working day, or sooner when a measurement lands that changes a tile. **Length.** Under 200 words. **Archive.** Every edition is posted to the [blog](https://leadgreen.ai/blog/) the same day, so the RSS feed carries them too.

**Own Your AI.** Prem Naraindas's fortnightly LinkedIn newsletter on sovereign AI will carry a three-line "meter" block with one reading from this index in every issue, from its next edition. The two do not overlap: Own Your AI is about control, this one is about energy.

# Bring a GPU, a red pen or a keyboard

> How to add a measurement, review a claim or write for Lead Green: the measurement protocol, the review rules, what is needed first and the licences.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/contribute/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/contribute/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Contribute*

Lead Green is small and it is public. Its value is the number of independent, reproducible measurements on the index and the care with which each one is checked. Both grow faster with volunteers. Here is what is needed, how to do it, and the rules that keep a row defensible.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Contribute. https://leadgreen.ai/contribute/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

*Roles*

## Five ways to help  Measurers

### Run the protocol

You have access to a GPU server, on-premise or rented, and can run a serving engine under a fixed load for an hour. You produce rows. Reviewers

### Check the working

You can read a benchmark's method, recompute a figure from its raw file, and say whether a claim on the site survives contact with its source. Writers

### Explain one question

You can take one of the upcoming blog topics, or propose one, and write it with the working shown and every figure sourced. Translators

### Carry it across

The carbon table was chosen for readers in the Gulf, South Asia, South-East Asia and Central Europe. Translations of the index and the "why" page, checked by a second speaker, are welcome. Developers

### API and MCP

The build script, the JSON API and the MCP server are small Python. A hosted MCP endpoint and a per-model comparison tool are open.

*How*

## Issues and pull requests

Everything lives in [the repository](https://github.com/katonic-dev/leadgreen-ai): the page sources, the build script, the dated data snapshots, the API and the MCP server. Propose a change as a pull request, or open an issue if you want to discuss it first. A measurement is submitted as a JSON file in the [measurement schema](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/schema/measurement.schema.json) plus the logs it was computed from; a correction is submitted with a link to the primary source. If you would rather not open a pull request, send a measurement or a correction to [hello@leadgreen.ai](mailto:hello@leadgreen.ai); it will be added under your name.

Contributors are credited by name on the change record and, for measurements, on the row itself. Bylines on blog posts are the author's own.

*Measurement protocol v0.2*

## How to produce a row that can sit beside the public ones

1. **Serving engine.** vLLM, the engine the public benchmark uses, so rows are comparable. Record the exact version. Other engines are welcome as clearly labelled separate rows. The public rows were made with vLLM 0.11.1 and the server flags in the benchmark's configs (max-num-batched-tokens 8192, max-model-len 20480, dtype bfloat16); record yours.
2. **Hardware.** Name the GPU model, memory, form factor (SXM, PCIe, NVL), count, any MIG profile and the weight precision (BF16, FP8, INT4). Name the driver and CUDA versions and the host. If the card is shared with anything else, say so.
3. **Prompt set.** A fixed, published prompt set with a stated average prompt length, linked or attached so another measurer can repeat it. To match the public rows, use the benchmark's own sample: lmarena-ai/arena-human-preference-100k (train), field conversation_a, one request per turn with the full history as the prompt, 1,024 requests, seed 0, as in the benchmark's datasets.py; for Qwen 3 pass chat_template_kwargs enable_thinking false. Or run the [benchmark harness](https://github.com/ml-energy/benchmark) itself and submit its output.
4. **Load.** Send at least 1,000 requests with the server's max_num_seqs as the only cap. The window starts when max_num_seqs requests have returned a first token and ends when all but max_num_seqs + 1 requests have finished (the public benchmark's rule); it must last at least five minutes, so send more requests at high concurrency. Record the average running batch the server actually held (vLLM's `num_requests_running`, scraped every second inside the window and averaged), not only the cap.
5. **Energy.** Read the GPU energy counter at the start and end of the window for every card (DCGM field 156, `DCGM_FI_DEV_TOTAL_ENERGY_CONSUMPTION`, millijoules); it is the counter the public benchmark reads through Zeus. Also log board power (field 155, `DCGM_FI_DEV_BOARD_POWER_WATTS`) every second for the average power column. If you only have `nvidia-smi`, sample `power.draw` every second, integrate, and say so.
6. **Latency and tokens.** Use a client that records the time of every streamed token, such as `vllm bench serve` with `--save-result`, which reports median and p99 inter-token latency, and attach its JSON. Read `vllm:generation_tokens_total` at both ends of the window, and record the average output length and the average prompt length.
7. **Report.** Joules per output token (energy ÷ output tokens), Wh per million (× 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600), median and p99 inter-token latency, tokens per second, average power summed across cards, and the fields above, in the [measurement schema](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/schema/measurement.schema.json); the example file `build/data/measurements/2026-09-26-example-qwen-3-14b-h100-3g40gb-x2.json` has every field filled. The build validates every file against the schema and refuses to publish one that fails. Attach the power log and the engine's metrics log; strip request bodies from engine logs, or link the prompt set instead of reproducing it. A row is comparable with the index only if its median inter-token latency is at or under 500 ms.
8. **Repeat.** Two runs; report both and the mean. If joules per output token differ by more than 5 percent between runs, say why or run a third.

The protocol measures GPU energy only, like the index. If you also have facility or host power, report it as separate fields; do not fold it in. The same goes for water: if you know the site's water use, report it in the optional site water field as water usage effectiveness (litres per kWh of IT energy, ISO/IEC 30134-9), never folded into Wh/M. Power for a sliced card is the whole card's; no tool reports power per slice. Load every slice with the same workload at the same time, read the card's energy exactly as for an unsliced card, and report Wh/M for the card with `mig_profile`, `slice_count` and `slices_loaded`. Never divide the card's power by the slice count, and never report a slice measured while the other slices sit idle. Compare a sliced run with the same person's whole-card run on the same card in the same session; the public 1 × H100 rows are the reference.

*Review rules*

## What it takes to land on the index

- **Two reviewers** for a new row or a changed figure, one of whom recomputes the number from the attached logs or the source file. The reviewers are two named reviewers, listed here before the first contributed row is accepted. Any row Katonic measures is also checked by a named reviewer with no Katonic affiliation, to be named here before the first Katonic row is published. A decision within 30 days.
- **Where accepted rows go.** Accepted rows are served at [`/api/v1/measurements.json`](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/measurements.json) with contributor, affiliation, measured_on, engine_version, driver_version and mig_profile on each row, and listed on the index under [Contributed measurements](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#contributed) with the contributor's name. They are never merged into the index table. A contributed row states its median inter-token latency; rows above 500 ms are shown and flagged.
- **Source snapshot.** Every public figure is taken from a dated copy of the source file, kept with the site, so it can be recomputed later even if the source moves.
- **Claims ledger.** Every figure on every page has a source and a retrieval date in the sources list. If it cannot be sourced, it does not ship.
- **Corrections** are made in the open: the change record on the index names what changed, when and why, and a corrected blog post keeps a note at the top.
- **Vendor rows are labelled.** A measurement made by or paid for by a hardware, cloud or model vendor is marked as such and shown separately from independent rows.
- **No customer names.** A measurement from a production site is described by hardware and workload, not by whose site it is.

*Needed first*

## The gaps, in order

1. **MIG slices.** Any model on a 1g, 2g or 3g slice of an H100 or H200, against the same model on the same whole card, measured by the same person in the same session with the same engine, driver and prompt set. Nothing public exists. The API's 1 × H100 rows are the public reference: for Qwen 3 14B in BF16, 196.1 Wh/M at a cap of 8 down to 31.1 at 256.
2. **Other GPUs.** A100, H200, L40S, and AMD MI300X. The index has H100 and B200 only.
3. **Hourly grid data.** Annual averages hide a lot. Hourly intensity for the grids on the carbon table, from a source whose licence allows republishing.
4. **Translations.** Arabic, Serbian, Traditional Chinese, Tagalog and Sinhala first, for the readers the carbon table was built for.
5. **Water.** Site water use beside any contributed row, as its own field. The index has none, and the two public per-prompt figures are measured on different boundaries and units of work.
6. **Reviews.** A second pair of eyes on any figure on the site, starting with the ones that get cited most.

*Licences*

## What you give and what you get

Code (the build script, the API generator, the MCP server) is Apache 2.0. Data and text (the compiled index, derived figures, page text, blog posts) are CC BY 4.0. By contributing you agree your contribution is offered under the same terms: your row and your logs are CC BY 4.0, and prompt sets keep their own licence. Sign commits with a Developer Certificate of Origin line (`Signed-off-by`). Public sources keep their own licences, which are listed per source and never overridden.
