*Trend*

## Sri Lanka's grid, year by year

From 2023 to 2025 the intensity fell 9 percent, from 416.9 to 379.3 gCO2e per kWh. The table uses 2024, the latest year with a value for every listed grid; on the 2025 figure the reference row would carry 24.1 kg per billion tokens.

*Ember yearly emissions intensity for Sri Lanka, and the reference row priced on each year*

| Year | g CO2e per kWh | kg CO2e per billion tokens, reference row |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 416.9 | 26.5 |
| 2024 | 392.8 | 24.9 |
| 2025 | 379.3 | 24.1 |

Lifecycle emissions intensity: CO2e per kWh of net generation, built from per-technology lifecycle factors (IPCC AR5 WG3 Annex III midpoints, all gases at GWP-100), so upstream methane, supply chains and plant manufacture are included. Production-based: imports and grid losses are excluded. A location-based figure for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported. A GPU server draws much the same power around the clock, while an annual average weights each hour by its generation, so on a grid whose clean supply peaks at midday a flat load sees a higher figure than the average.

## Which line it goes on

For GPUs you run in Sri Lanka, the electricity is your own consumption: it goes into your ESRS E1-5 energy total and its emissions into E1-6 as Scope 2, location-based, which is the method this page's figure matches. The market-based figure nets your contracted supply and needs your own contracts. Tokens bought from a hosted API are the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3 category 1, and sit outside your E1-5 line; [the why page](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) lists what to ask the provider. Ember's figure is a lifecycle intensity for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported.

At the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh per million output tokens, GPU only), about 24.9 grams of CO2e per million tokens, or 24.9 kg per billion, on Sri Lanka's 2024 grid. Across the index the range is 5.1 to 225.1 kg per billion tokens. A lightly loaded server sits above these floors, and host, network and cooling are not counted.

### Is running AI in Sri Lanka cleaner than the world average?

Sri Lanka's 2024 intensity of 393 gCO2e per kWh is 1.2× cleaner than the world average of 473 (473 gCO2e per kWh). The same tokens on the same GPUs produce the same energy figure anywhere; only the carbon figure moves with the grid.

As a comparison, not as a filing. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Grids](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) · Europe · a reference grid*

An LLM served on Germany's grid emits about **21.6 kg CO2e per billion output tokens**, 21.6 g per million, at the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh/M), GPU energy only; the index's lowest row emits 4.4 kg and its highest 194.7 kg. The grid ran at **340 gCO2e per kWh** in 2024 on Ember's yearly figures, 1.4× cleaner than the world average of 473, and 73rd of the 193 countries Ember covers, counting from the cleanest. Energy per token does not change with geography; carbon per token does.

**Area** Germany (DEU, DE). **Basis** lifecycle, location-based, annual average. **Data** [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

- **Grid intensity, 2024:** 340 gCO2e/kWh Ember yearly data, lifecycle, location-based. World: 473.
- **Reference row, per billion tokens:** 21.6 kg CO2e Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh/M, GPU only, a floor.
- **Rank:** 73 of 193 1 is the cleanest grid Ember covers (Ethiopia, 23); 193 the highest (Turkmenistan, 1,306).

Carbon per token is energy per token times the grid. The energy figures here are GPU-only floors from a busy server; a lightly loaded deployment sits above them, and so does anything that includes the host, the network and the cooling. Wh/M × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000 gives kg CO2e per billion output tokens.

*Trend*

## Germany's grid, year by year

From 2023 to 2025 the intensity fell 8 percent, from 363.6 to 334.1 gCO2e per kWh. The table uses 2024, the latest year with a value for every listed grid; on the 2025 figure the reference row would carry 21.2 kg per billion tokens.

*Ember yearly emissions intensity for Germany, and the reference row priced on each year*

| Year | g CO2e per kWh | kg CO2e per billion tokens, reference row |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 363.6 | 23.1 |
| 2024 | 339.9 | 21.6 |
| 2025 | 334.1 | 21.2 |

Lifecycle emissions intensity: CO2e per kWh of net generation, built from per-technology lifecycle factors (IPCC AR5 WG3 Annex III midpoints, all gases at GWP-100), so upstream methane, supply chains and plant manufacture are included. Production-based: imports and grid losses are excluded. A location-based figure for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported. A GPU server draws much the same power around the clock, while an annual average weights each hour by its generation, so on a grid whose clean supply peaks at midday a flat load sees a higher figure than the average.

*Every model*

Each model's lowest index row, GPU only, at the most energy-efficient configuration measured, multiplied by 340 gCO2e per kWh. The spread from the lowest row to the highest is 44×, and it is entirely the model, the GPU and the load; the grid multiplies all of them alike.

*Reporting*

## Which line it goes on

For GPUs you run in Germany, the electricity is your own consumption: it goes into your ESRS E1-5 energy total and its emissions into E1-6 as Scope 2, location-based, which is the method this page's figure matches. The market-based figure nets your contracted supply and needs your own contracts. Tokens bought from a hosted API are the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3 category 1, and sit outside your E1-5 line; [the why page](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) lists what to ask the provider. Ember's figure is a lifecycle intensity for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported.

*Questions*

## Asked about AI carbon in Germany

### What is the grid carbon intensity of Germany?

340 gCO2e per kWh in 2024, on Ember's yearly electricity data: a lifecycle, location-based figure for the country's own generation, 1.4× cleaner than the world average of 473. Ember's 2025 figure is 334.1.

### How much CO2 does a million AI tokens produce in Germany?

At the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh per million output tokens, GPU only), about 21.6 grams of CO2e per million tokens, or 21.6 kg per billion, on Germany's 2024 grid. Across the index the range is 4.4 to 194.7 kg per billion tokens. A lightly loaded server sits above these floors, and host, network and cooling are not counted.

### Is running AI in Germany cleaner than the world average?

Germany's 2024 intensity of 340 gCO2e per kWh is 1.4× cleaner than the world average of 473 (473 gCO2e per kWh). The same tokens on the same GPUs produce the same energy figure anywhere; only the carbon figure moves with the grid.

### Can I use this figure for my Scope 2 report in Germany?

As a comparison, not as a filing. Ember's intensity is a lifecycle figure on net generation, not a Scope 2 combustion factor, and it is location-based; a market-based figure needs your own contracted supply. Tokens bought from a hosted API land in your Scope 3 category 1, not your Scope 2. The why page explains both.

### Where do these figures come from?

Grid intensity: Ember, Yearly electricity data, October 2026 release (2024; 2023, 2024, 2025 shown), CC BY 4.0, retrieved 17 October 2026. Energy per token: the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026). Carbon is Wh/M × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000.

*Sources*

## Where every figure came from

Grid intensity: [Ember, Yearly electricity data](https://ember-energy.org/data/yearly-electricity-data/), October 2026 release, emissions intensity of total generation, 2023, 2024, 2025 (CC BY 4.0), retrieved 17 October 2026. Energy per token: [ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).

*Reporting*

## Which line it goes on

For GPUs you run in Ireland, the electricity is your own consumption: it goes into your ESRS E1-5 energy total and its emissions into E1-6 as Scope 2, location-based, which is the method this page's figure matches. The market-based figure nets your contracted supply and needs your own contracts. Tokens bought from a hosted API are the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3 category 1, and sit outside your E1-5 line; [the why page](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) lists what to ask the provider. Ember's figure is a lifecycle intensity for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported.

*Questions*

## Asked about AI carbon in Ireland

### What is the grid carbon intensity of Ireland?

271 gCO2e per kWh in 2024, on Ember's yearly electricity data: a lifecycle, location-based figure for the country's own generation, 1.7× cleaner than the world average of 473. Ember's 2025 figure is 263.3.

### How much CO2 does a million AI tokens produce in Ireland?

At the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh per million output tokens, GPU only), about 17.2 grams of CO2e per million tokens, or 17.2 kg per billion, on Ireland's 2024 grid. Across the index the range is 3.5 to 155.1 kg per billion tokens. A lightly loaded server sits above these floors, and host, network and cooling are not counted.

### Is running AI in Ireland cleaner than the world average?

Ireland's 2024 intensity of 271 gCO2e per kWh is 1.7× cleaner than the world average of 473 (473 gCO2e per kWh). The same tokens on the same GPUs produce the same energy figure anywhere; only the carbon figure moves with the grid.

### Can I use this figure for my Scope 2 report in Ireland?

As a comparison, not as a filing. Ember's intensity is a lifecycle figure on net generation, not a Scope 2 combustion factor, and it is location-based; a market-based figure needs your own contracted supply. Tokens bought from a hosted API land in your Scope 3 category 1, not your Scope 2. The why page explains both.

### Where do these figures come from?

Grid intensity: Ember, Yearly electricity data, October 2026 release (2024; 2023, 2024, 2025 shown), CC BY 4.0, retrieved 17 October 2026. Energy per token: the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026). Carbon is Wh/M × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000.

*Sources*

## Where every figure came from

Grid intensity: [Ember, Yearly electricity data](https://ember-energy.org/data/yearly-electricity-data/), October 2026 release, emissions intensity of total generation, 2023, 2024, 2025 (CC BY 4.0), retrieved 17 October 2026. Energy per token: [ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).

The grid ran at **216 gCO2e per kWh** in 2024 on Ember's yearly figures, 2.2× cleaner than the world average of 473, and 50th of the 193 countries Ember covers, counting from the cleanest. *Trend*

## United Kingdom's grid, year by year

From 2023 to 2025 the intensity fell 7 percent, from 235.6 to 218.2 gCO2e per kWh. The table uses 2024, the latest year with a value for every listed grid; on the 2025 figure the reference row would carry 13.8 kg per billion tokens.

*Ember yearly emissions intensity for United Kingdom, and the reference row priced on each year*

| Year | g CO2e per kWh | kg CO2e per billion tokens, reference row |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 235.6 | 15.0 |
| 2024 | 216.5 | 13.7 |
| 2025 | 218.2 | 13.8 |

Lifecycle emissions intensity: CO2e per kWh of net generation, built from per-technology lifecycle factors (IPCC AR5 WG3 Annex III midpoints, all gases at GWP-100), so upstream methane, supply chains and plant manufacture are included. Production-based: imports and grid losses are excluded. A location-based figure for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported. A GPU server draws much the same power around the clock, while an annual average weights each hour by its generation, so on a grid whose clean supply peaks at midday a flat load sees a higher figure than the average.

Every configuration of every model, not only the lowest row, is on [the model pages](https://leadgreen.ai/models/); the [MCP server](https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/) prices any of them on Hungary's grid for a token count you give it.

*Reporting*

## Which line it goes on

For GPUs you run in Hungary, the electricity is your own consumption: it goes into your ESRS E1-5 energy total and its emissions into E1-6 as Scope 2, location-based, which is the method this page's figure matches. The market-based figure nets your contracted supply and needs your own contracts. Tokens bought from a hosted API are the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3 category 1, and sit outside your E1-5 line; [the why page](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) lists what to ask the provider. Ember's figure is a lifecycle intensity for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported.

*Questions*

## Asked about AI carbon in Hungary

### What is the grid carbon intensity of Hungary?

184 gCO2e per kWh in 2024, on Ember's yearly electricity data: a lifecycle, location-based figure for the country's own generation, 2.6× cleaner than the world average of 473. Ember's 2025 figure is 162.6.

### How much CO2 does a million AI tokens produce in Hungary?

At the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh per million output tokens, GPU only), about 11.7 grams of CO2e per million tokens, or 11.7 kg per billion, on Hungary's 2024 grid. Across the index the range is 2.4 to 105.4 kg per billion tokens. A lightly loaded server sits above these floors, and host, network and cooling are not counted.

### Is running AI in Hungary cleaner than the world average?

Hungary's 2024 intensity of 184 gCO2e per kWh is 2.6× cleaner than the world average of 473 (473 gCO2e per kWh). The same tokens on the same GPUs produce the same energy figure anywhere; only the carbon figure moves with the grid.

### Can I use this figure for my Scope 2 report in Hungary?

As a comparison, not as a filing. Ember's intensity is a lifecycle figure on net generation, not a Scope 2 combustion factor, and it is location-based; a market-based figure needs your own contracted supply. Tokens bought from a hosted API land in your Scope 3 category 1, not your Scope 2. The why page explains both.

### Where do these figures come from?

Grid intensity: Ember, Yearly electricity data, October 2026 release (2024; 2023, 2024, 2025 shown), CC BY 4.0, retrieved 17 October 2026. Energy per token: the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026). Carbon is Wh/M × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000.

*Sources*

## Where every figure came from

Grid intensity: [Ember, Yearly electricity data](https://ember-energy.org/data/yearly-electricity-data/), October 2026 release, emissions intensity of total generation, 2023, 2024, 2025 (CC BY 4.0), retrieved 17 October 2026. Energy per token: [ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).

GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Grids](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) · Oceania · a market Katonic sells in or expects to*

An LLM served on New Zealand's grid emits about **7.1 kg CO2e per billion output tokens**, 7.1 g per million, at the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh/M), GPU energy only; the index's lowest row emits 1.5 kg and its highest 64.1 kg. The grid ran at **112 gCO2e per kWh** in 2024 on Ember's yearly figures, 4.2× cleaner than the world average of 473, and 27th of the 193 countries Ember covers, counting from the cleanest. Energy per token does not change with geography; carbon per token does.

Carbon per token is energy per token times the grid. The energy figures here are GPU-only floors from a busy server; a lightly loaded deployment sits above them, and so does anything that includes the host, the network and the cooling. Wh/M × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000 gives kg CO2e per billion output tokens.

*Trend*

## New Zealand's grid, year by year

From 2023 to 2025 the intensity rose 5 percent, from 87.4 to 92.1 gCO2e per kWh. The table uses 2024, the latest year with a value for every listed grid; on the 2025 figure the reference row would carry 5.8 kg per billion tokens.

*Ember yearly emissions intensity for New Zealand, and the reference row priced on each year*

| Year | g CO2e per kWh | kg CO2e per billion tokens, reference row |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 87.4 | 5.5 |
| 2024 | 111.9 | 7.1 |
| 2025 | 92.1 | 5.8 |

Lifecycle emissions intensity: CO2e per kWh of net generation, built from per-technology lifecycle factors (IPCC AR5 WG3 Annex III midpoints, all gases at GWP-100), so upstream methane, supply chains and plant manufacture are included. Production-based: imports and grid losses are excluded. A location-based figure for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported. A GPU server draws much the same power around the clock, while an annual average weights each hour by its generation, so on a grid whose clean supply peaks at midday a flat load sees a higher figure than the average.

Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. # France: the carbon of AI inference per billion tokens

Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Grids](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) · Europe · a reference grid*

An LLM served on France's grid emits about **2.6 kg CO2e per billion output tokens**, 2.6 g per million, at the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh/M), GPU energy only; the index's lowest row emits 0.5 kg and its highest 23.1 kg. The grid ran at **40 gCO2e per kWh** in 2024 on Ember's yearly figures, 11.7× cleaner than the world average of 473, and 12th of the 193 countries Ember covers, counting from the cleanest. Energy per token does not change with geography; carbon per token does.

Carbon per token is energy per token times the grid. The energy figures here are GPU-only floors from a busy server; a lightly loaded deployment sits above them, and so does anything that includes the host, the network and the cooling. Wh/M × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000 gives kg CO2e per billion output tokens.

*Trend*

## France's grid, year by year

From 2023 to 2025 the intensity fell 23 percent, from 53.3 to 41.2 gCO2e per kWh. The table uses 2024, the latest year with a value for every listed grid; on the 2025 figure the reference row would carry 2.6 kg per billion tokens.

*Ember yearly emissions intensity for France, and the reference row priced on each year*

| Year | g CO2e per kWh | kg CO2e per billion tokens, reference row |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | 53.3 | 3.4 |
| 2024 | 40.3 | 2.6 |
| 2025 | 41.2 | 2.6 |

Lifecycle emissions intensity: CO2e per kWh of net generation, built from per-technology lifecycle factors (IPCC AR5 WG3 Annex III midpoints, all gases at GWP-100), so upstream methane, supply chains and plant manufacture are included. Production-based: imports and grid losses are excluded. A location-based figure for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported. A GPU server draws much the same power around the clock, while an annual average weights each hour by its generation, so on a grid whose clean supply peaks at midday a flat load sees a higher figure than the average.

*Reporting*

## Which line it goes on

For GPUs you run in France, the electricity is your own consumption: it goes into your ESRS E1-5 energy total and its emissions into E1-6 as Scope 2, location-based, which is the method this page's figure matches. The market-based figure nets your contracted supply and needs your own contracts. Tokens bought from a hosted API are the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3 category 1, and sit outside your E1-5 line; [the why page](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#hosted) lists what to ask the provider. Ember's figure is a lifecycle intensity for comparing places, not a Scope 2 combustion factor to file as reported.

*Questions*

## Asked about AI carbon in France

### What is the grid carbon intensity of France?

40 gCO2e per kWh in 2024, on Ember's yearly electricity data: a lifecycle, location-based figure for the country's own generation, 11.7× cleaner than the world average of 473. Ember's 2025 figure is 41.2.

### How much CO2 does a million AI tokens produce in France?

At the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh per million output tokens, GPU only), about 2.6 grams of CO2e per million tokens, or 2.6 kg per billion, on France's 2024 grid. Across the index the range is 0.5 to 23.1 kg per billion tokens. A lightly loaded server sits above these floors, and host, network and cooling are not counted.

### Is running AI in France cleaner than the world average?

France's 2024 intensity of 40 gCO2e per kWh is 11.7× cleaner than the world average of 473 (473 gCO2e per kWh). The same tokens on the same GPUs produce the same energy figure anywhere; only the carbon figure moves with the grid.

### Can I use this figure for my Scope 2 report in France?

As a comparison, not as a filing. Ember's intensity is a lifecycle figure on net generation, not a Scope 2 combustion factor, and it is location-based; a market-based figure needs your own contracted supply. Tokens bought from a hosted API land in your Scope 3 category 1, not your Scope 2. The why page explains both.

# H100 vs B200: GPU energy per million output tokens

> B200 vs H100: the B200 uses a median 39 percent less GPU energy per output token across 14 open-weight models (1.05× to 4.55×). ML.ENERGY v3.0.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Two generations · 14 models*

On the index the B200 uses a median **39 percent less** GPU energy per output token than the H100, across all 14 open-weight models measured on both cards: the H100 row uses 1.63× the B200 row's energy at the median, from **4.55×** (Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct) down to **1.05×** (NVIDIA Nemotron Nano 9B V2). Part of many gaps is the sweep rather than the silicon: the two rows of a pair often differ in card count and running batch, and on eight of the 14 pairs the B200 row holds the model on fewer cards. The leaderboard's own analysis of the wider sweep agrees: across three latency limits the B200 wins 63 of 72 comparisons with a median 35 percent less energy per token ([arXiv:2601.22076](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22076)).

**Unit** watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M). GPU only, busy server. Every row is a floor. **Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. H100 vs B200: which uses less GPU energy per token? 14 models. https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The 14 pairs](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#pairs)
- [The sweep](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#sweep)
- [Power against energy](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#power)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#sources)

- **Widest gap:** 4.55 × Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct: 303.5 Wh/M on 8 × H100 against 66.7 on 4 × B200.
- **Median gap, 14 pairs:** 1.63 × H100 row energy per token over B200 row energy per token, at each model's index rows.
- **Narrowest gap:** 1.05 × NVIDIA Nemotron Nano 9B V2: 43.1 Wh/M on 1 × H100 against 40.9 on 1 × B200.

Each pair compares a model's index row on the H100 with its index row on the B200: the lowest-energy configuration the leaderboard measured on each card, at or under 500 ms median inter-token latency. The ratio is the H100 row's energy per token over the B200 row's.

*The pairs*

## Every model measured on both cards

*Index rows paired by model, with card count and running batch, sorted by the gap*

| Model | H100 | Running batch | Wh / M | B200 | Running batch | Wh / M | H100 ÷ B200 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct/) | 8 × H100 | 228 | 303.5 | 4 × B200 | 3,765 | 66.7 | 4.55× |
| [Qwen 3 14B](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-14b/) | 1 × H100 | 253 | 31.1 | 1 × B200 | 2,045 | 15.2 | 2.04× |
| [Llama 3.1 70B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-1-70b-instruct/) | 4 × H100 | 898 | 103.7 | 2 × B200 | 2,042 | 52.4 | 1.98× |
| [Llama 3.3 70B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-3-70b-instruct/) | 4 × H100 | 724 | 117.5 | 2 × B200 | 1,022 | 60.7 | 1.94× |
| [Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-1-405b-instruct-fp8/) | 8 × H100 | 255 | 572.9 | 4 × B200 | 510 | 318.5 | 1.80× |
| [Gemma 3 12B](https://leadgreen.ai/models/gemma-3-12b/) | 1 × H100 | 128 | 46.1 | 1 × B200 | 487 | 26.5 | 1.74× |
| [Gemma 3 27B](https://leadgreen.ai/models/gemma-3-27b/) | 2 × H100 | 187 | 80.4 | 1 × B200 | 247 | 49.1 | 1.64× |
| [Qwen 3 32B](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-32b/) | 2 × H100 | 256 | 63.5 | 1 × B200 | 383 | 39.1 | 1.63× |
| [Qwen 3 30B A3B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-30b-a3b-instruct/) | 2 × H100 | 1,019 | 24.7 | 1 × B200 | 1,023 | 15.7 | 1.58× |
| [Llama 3.1 8B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-1-8b-instruct/) | 1 × H100 | 511 | 19.5 | 1 × B200 | 2,043 | 13.0 | 1.50× |
| [Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-fp8/) | 8 × H100 | 511 | 206.0 | 2 × B200 | 256 | 139.1 | 1.48× |
| [Qwen 3 8B](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-8b/) | 1 × H100 | 474 | 20.0 | 1 × B200 | 1,427 | 14.7 | 1.36× |
| [NVIDIA Nemotron Nano 12B V2](https://leadgreen.ai/models/nvidia-nemotron-nano-12b-v2/) | 1 × H100 | 241 | 50.1 | 1 × B200 | 256 | 39.4 | 1.27× |
| [NVIDIA Nemotron Nano 9B V2](https://leadgreen.ai/models/nvidia-nemotron-nano-9b-v2/) | 1 × H100 | 255 | 43.1 | 1 × B200 | 255 | 40.9 | 1.05× |

Running batch (avg) is the average number of requests the server was decoding at once over the steady-state window (vLLM's `num_requests_running`). Model names link to every measured configuration of that model.

*The sweep*

## How much of the gap is the silicon

The gap also depends on which configurations were swept. The 4.55× pair compares an H100 row that was run only at eight cards and a cap of at most 256 requests with a B200 row at a running batch of 3,765 on four cards; at the same cap of 256 the B200 row reads 197.5 Wh/M against the H100's 303.5, a gap of 1.54×. The two Nemotron pairs compare runs whose average answers are 3.2 and 2.4 times longer on the B200 (462 and 510 tokens on the H100 against 1,464 and 1,242).

At a 50 ms ceiling the comparison shifts: 14 models still have a row on both cards, and the H100 uses less energy per token than the B200 on two of them (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 19.5 Wh/M on 1 × H100 against 19.6 on 1 × B200; Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8, 306.7 Wh/M on 8 × H100 against 408.9 on 2 × B200).

Every configuration behind these rows is on [the model pages](https://leadgreen.ai/models/) and in the [API](https://leadgreen.ai/api/), so any pair can be re-cut at a matched cap or a matched running batch.

*Power against energy*

## The card that draws more can use less

A B200 card draws more power than an H100: NVIDIA rates the H100 SXM at up to 700 W and the B200 configurable up to 1,000 W, and on these index rows the cards averaged 612 W per H100 and 868 W per B200. It uses less energy per token because it finishes more tokens in each second of that draw. Power tells you the size of the feed; energy per token tells you what the feed produced. An eight-GPU DGX B200 is rated at about 14.3 kW against 8.0 kW for its GPUs, so the system draws 1.79× what the cards do; the [method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method) takes a GPU figure to the facility meter.

*Maximum thermal design power, as published by NVIDIA*

| GPU | Form | Max TDP | Memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| A100 80GB | SXM | 400 W | 80 GB HBM2e |
| A100 80GB | PCIe | 300 W | 80 GB HBM2e |
| H100 | SXM | up to 700 W | 80 GB HBM3 |
| H100 | NVL | 350 to 400 W | 94 GB HBM3 |
| H200 | SXM | up to 700 W | 141 GB HBM3e |
| H200 | NVL | up to 600 W | 141 GB HBM3e |
| B200 | HGX, SXM6 | configurable up to 1,000 W | 180 GB HBM3e |

*Questions*

## Asked about H100 against B200

### Is the B200 more energy-efficient than the H100 for LLM inference?

On the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's index rows, yes for all 14 models measured on both:

### How much energy does a B200 save over an H100 per million tokens?

It depends on the model: for the reference model, Qwen 3 32B, the index rows are 63.5 Wh/M on 2 × H100 against 39.1 Wh/M on 1 × B200. The table on this page gives all 14 pairs.

### Does the B200 draw more power than the H100?

A B200 card draws more power than an H100: NVIDIA rates the H100 SXM at up to 700 W and the B200 configurable up to 1,000 W, and on these index rows the cards averaged 612 W per H100 and 868 W per B200. It uses less energy per token because it finishes more tokens in each second of that draw. Power tells you the size of the feed; energy per token tells you what the feed produced.

### Should I buy B200s to cut the energy of AI inference?

Not first. The same model on the same H100 cards moves 7.1× in energy per token between a running batch of 8 and 256, which is more than the widest generation gap here (4.55×). Consolidating traffic onto fewer, busier cards costs nothing in hardware; the generation change comes after.

### Why do the two rows of a pair have different card counts?

The leaderboard picks each GPU's configurations separately; a B200 has more memory, so a model that needs eight H100s can fit fewer B200s. On 8 of the 14 pairs the B200 row holds the model on fewer cards, and the running batches differ too, so the ratio compares the best measured row on each card, not like for like.

### Where do these figures come from?

The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026, retrieved 26 September 2026), Text Conversation task, GPU energy measured with Zeus under vLLM on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; each row is the lowest-energy configuration at or under 500 ms median inter-token latency. TDP figures are NVIDIA's published specifications.

*Sources*

## Where every figure came from

[ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).

Corroboration: Chung et al. (The ML.ENERGY Initiative, University of Michigan), *Where Do the Joules Go? Diagnosing Inference Energy Consumption*, [arXiv:2601.22076](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22076) (v2, January 2026), the leaderboard team's analysis of the same measurements across 46 models and 1,858 configurations: across three median inter-token latency limits the B200 wins 88 percent (63 of 72) of comparisons with a median 35 percent energy reduction, ranging from 53 percent more to 82 percent less. Retrieved 21 October 2026. This page's ratio is narrower in scope: one task, one latency limit, the index rows only.

TDP and memory: NVIDIA product specifications for [H100](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/) and [DGX B200](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/dgx-b200/), and the [HGX B200 product carbon footprint summary](https://images.nvidia.com/aem-dam/Solutions/documents/HGX-B200-PCF-Summary.pdf) (July 2025), retrieved 26 September 2026.

# How much energy does an AI query use?

> An AI query uses about 0.24 to 0.34 Wh by four published whole-stack figures; the GPU share on this index is 0.005 to 0.21 Wh an answer.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[The index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/) · Per query*

An AI chatbot query uses about **0.24 to 0.34 Wh** of electricity across the whole serving stack, by four published whole-stack figures: Google 0.24 Wh per median Gemini Apps text prompt (August 2025), Epoch AI 0.3 Wh per typical 500-token ChatGPT reply (February 2025), OpenAI 0.34 Wh per average query (June 2025) and Microsoft Research's modelled median of 0.31 Wh for a frontier-scale model on H100 nodes (interquartile range 0.16 to 0.60 Wh, June 2026). The GPU share of one answer on this index runs from **0.005 to 0.21 Wh** by model and GPU, measured on busy servers. One answer from a busy open-weight model costs about **0.040 Wh** of GPU energy on the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100: 63.5 Wh per million output tokens, answers averaging 634 tokens, 256 requests in flight). Of Google's 0.24 Wh the accelerators are 58 percent, and its narrow accelerator-only figure is 0.10 Wh. The gap between a per-prompt figure and a per-million-tokens figure is boundary, load and answer length, and this page converts one into the other with each of them stated.

**Units** watt-hours per answer (Wh) and watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M). Wh per answer = Wh/M × output tokens ÷ 1,000,000. **Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [per-query.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/per-query.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. How much energy does an AI query use? Per prompt against per million tokens. https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The bridge](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#bridge)
- [What vendors published](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#published)
- [Batch size one](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#batch-one)
- [To a budget](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#budget)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#sources)

- **One answer, reference row:** 0.040 Wh Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh/M × 634 output tokens. GPU only, busy server, a floor.
- **Google, median prompt:** 0.24 Wh Gemini Apps text prompt, August 2025, whole stack: accelerators 58 percent (0.14 Wh), narrow accelerator-only figure 0.10 Wh.
- **AI Energy Score, one query:** 0.0042 to 1.27 Wh 22 models, batch size 1, answers fixed at ten tokens, H100 80GB, December 2025 round. A probe, not a serving load.

Three kinds of figure are quoted as "the energy of an AI query", and they do not share a boundary or a load. The index's rows are GPU energy per million output tokens from a busy server. Vendors' per-prompt figures count a whole serving estate. The AI Energy Score runs one query at a time with a fixed ten-token answer. Each is a real measurement; the table below puts the first kind in per-answer units so it can sit beside the others.

*The bridge*

## From watt-hours per million tokens to watt-hours per answer

Energy per answer is energy per token times the answer's length. Each row below takes a measured Wh/M figure and the average output length the benchmark recorded on that row, and multiplies them. The result is what one average answer on that row cost in GPU energy.

*Measured rows converted to GPU watt-hours per answer, using each row's own average output length*

| Row | Model | GPUs | Running batch | Wh / M | Output tokens | Wh per answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Index, lowest row | [Llama 3.1 8B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-1-8b-instruct/) | 1 × B200 | 2,043 | 13.0 | 396 | 0.005 |
| Index, reference row | [Qwen 3 32B](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-32b/) | 2 × H100 | 256 | 63.5 | 634 | 0.040 |
| Same row, lightly loaded | [Qwen 3 32B](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-32b/) | 2 × H100 | 8 | 452.0 | 631 | 0.285 |
| Index, highest row | [Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-1-405b-instruct-fp8/) | 8 × H100 | 255 | 572.9 | 367 | 0.210 |
| Highest configuration measured | [Llama 3.1 405B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-1-405b-instruct/) | 8 × B200 | 8 | 6,073.4 | 363 | 2.207 |

Running batch is the average number of requests the server was decoding at once over the steady-state window (vLLM's `num_requests_running`). The first four rows are index rows or ladder rows at or under the 500 ms median inter-token latency ceiling; the last is the highest-energy configuration the leaderboard measured at all, kept to show the range a lightly loaded large model can reach. A kilowatt-hour serves about 24,800 answers at the reference row.

*What vendors published*

## Three per-prompt figures, and what they count

In August 2025 Google put the median Gemini Apps text prompt at **0.24 Wh**, 0.03 g CO2e and 0.26 mL of water. The figure counts the whole serving stack: the accelerators are 58 percent of it, about 0.14 Wh, and the host machines, idle capacity held for peaks and the data centre's overhead make up the rest. Google also reports a narrow, accelerator-only figure of 0.10 Wh, which is the boundary this index uses. So Google's own numbers say the stack multiplies the accelerator figure by 1.7× to 2.4×, depending on which accelerator figure is the base.

In July 2025 Mistral put a 400-token reply from its large model at 1.14 g CO2e and 45 mL of water, without a watt-hour figure, so it cannot be placed on an energy axis at all.

In June 2026 Microsoft Research (Oviedo et al., arXiv 2509.20241 v2) modelled the energy of a query to a frontier-scale model, over 200 billion parameters on H100 nodes, at a median of **0.31 Wh** with an interquartile range of 0.16 to 0.60 Wh, rising to 3.91 Wh for a long-reasoning query about fifteen times the typical length. It is a model of the serving stack, not a meter reading, and it states no running batch, so it sits beside Google's figure as a second whole-stack estimate and not as an index row.

None of the three states the model's serving load, and none gives an output length with a measured load behind it, so none converts to watt-hours per million tokens. Set beside the index on the narrow boundary, Google's 0.10 Wh is 2.5× the reference row's 0.040 Wh answer; the rest of the difference is a different model, a different load and an unstated answer length. Google's figure tells a hyperscaler's customers what a prompt costs across its estate. The index tells a buyer what a named model on named GPUs costs at a stated load, which is the figure a vendor can be held to because the buyer can measure it.

*Batch size one*

## The AI Energy Score measures a probe, not a serving load

The AI Energy Score reports GPU watt-hours for 1,000 text-generation queries run one at a time on NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs, with the answer fixed at ten tokens for non-reasoning models. Per query, its 22 December 2025 rows run from 0.0042 Wh (tencent/Hunyuan-1.8B-Instruct) to 1.27 Wh (zai-org/GLM-4.6). The index carries all of them in their own unit and does not convert them.

*AI Energy Score, text generation, December 2025 round, by class*

| Class | Fits | Models | Wh per 1,000 queries | Wh per query |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | fits one consumer GPU | 12 | 4.2 to 81.8 | 0.0042 to 0.082 |
| B | fits one H100 (single cloud GPU) | 3 | 37.4 to 54.5 | 0.0374 to 0.054 |
| C | needs more than one H100 (multiple cloud GPUs) | 7 | 36.6 to 1,273.5 | 0.0366 to 1.274 |

Dividing a batch-size-one figure by its ten tokens gives an energy per token for a card that is mostly waiting (tencent/Hunyuan-1.8B-Instruct would read 420 Wh/M), which is why the index refuses the conversion. Every row, with its star rating, is on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#per-query) and in [per-query.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/per-query.json).

*To a budget*

## Per answer is for intuition; per million tokens is for the plan

A per-answer figure makes the number legible: 0.040 Wh is a 10 W LED bulb for about 14 seconds (the bulb is a stated assumption, the tokens are measured). A budget needs the per-token form, because tokens are what the invoice counts. Monthly output tokens × Wh/M gives watt-hours; at the reference row a megawatt-hour of GPU energy serves 15.8 billion output tokens, and at the top of the concurrency ladder the same megawatt-hour serves 2.2 billion.

To take either figure to the facility meter, multiply by the system-to-GPU power ratio (1.79 for a DGX B200) and the site's PUE; with a PUE of 1.3 the reference row's 63.5 Wh/M becomes about 148 Wh/M at the meter. Both multipliers are the operator's own. The [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/) entry explains what sits inside and outside each figure.

*Questions*

## Asked about the energy of one query

### How much energy does an AI query use?

About 0.24 to 0.34 Wh across the whole serving stack, by the published figures from Google (0.24 Wh, August 2025), Epoch AI (0.3 Wh, February 2025), OpenAI (0.34 Wh, June 2025) and Microsoft Research (0.31 Wh, a modelled median for a frontier-scale model on H100 nodes, June 2026). Below that headline it depends on the model, the GPUs, how busy the server is and how long the answer runs, so a single figure needs those four stated. On the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh per million output tokens, 256 requests in flight), one answer of 634 tokens costs about 0.040 Wh of GPU energy. The same model on the same cards holding 8 requests costs about 0.29 Wh an answer. Google's published median for a Gemini Apps text prompt is 0.24 Wh across the whole serving stack (August 2025). These figures are GPU energy from a busy server unless stated otherwise; host, network and cooling sit outside them.

### Why is Google's 0.24 Wh per prompt higher than the index's figure?

Mostly boundary. Google counts the whole stack: the accelerators are 58 percent of its 0.24 Wh, about 0.14 Wh, with host machines, idle capacity held for peaks and data-centre overhead making up the rest, and it also publishes a narrow accelerator-only figure of 0.10 Wh. The index counts GPU energy only, at steady state on a busy server. On the narrow boundary Google's prompt is 2.5× the reference row's answer, and the two measure different models, loads and answer lengths. Neither figure is wrong; they answer different questions.

### How do I convert watt-hours per prompt into watt-hours per million tokens?

Divide the energy per answer by the answer's output tokens and multiply by a million: Wh/M = Wh per answer ÷ output tokens × 1,000,000. The reverse is Wh per answer = Wh/M × output tokens ÷ 1,000,000; the reference row's 63.5 Wh/M × 634 tokens gives 0.040 Wh. The conversion only holds when both figures share a boundary and a load. A per-prompt figure with no output length cannot be converted; Google's 0.24 Wh would read 378 Wh/M at the reference row's answer length and 158 Wh/M on its narrow boundary, but Google does not publish the prompt's token count, so those are illustrations, not figures.

### Can the AI Energy Score's Wh per 1,000 queries be converted to Wh per million tokens?

No. The AI Energy Score runs one query at a time (batch size 1) with the answer fixed at ten tokens for non-reasoning models, so the arithmetic (tencent/Hunyuan-1.8B-Instruct: 4.2 Wh per 1,000 queries ÷ 1,000 ÷ 10 tokens × 1,000,000 = 420 Wh/M) describes an idle card answering a ten-token probe, not a serving workload. The index keeps the AI Energy Score as a per-query measurement in its own table and does not mix the two units. The ML.ENERGY rows, measured on a busy server, are the ones in Wh/M.

### Does how busy the server is change the energy of one query?

More than anything else. Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 goes from 63.5 Wh/M at a running batch of 256 to 452 Wh/M at 8, 7.1× on the same hardware, because the cards draw only 39 percent more power serving 256 requests than 8. One answer goes from 0.040 Wh to about 0.29 Wh. A department assistant with a few users at a time sits at the top of that range.

### What about the carbon and water of one query?

Google puts the median Gemini Apps text prompt at 0.03 g CO2e and 0.26 mL of water (August 2025); Mistral puts a 400-token reply from its large model at 1.14 g CO2e and 45 mL (July 2025), without a watt-hour figure. For GPU-side carbon on the index, multiply Wh per answer by the grid's gCO2e per kWh: the reference row's answer carries about 0.028 g on Saudi Arabia's 2024 grid (689 gCO2e per kWh) and 0.0012 g on Norway's (30). The index measures electricity, not water.

*Sources*

# Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)

> The unit of the index: the GPU energy, in watt-hours, that a serving configuration uses to generate one million output tokens.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

13.0 to 572.9 Wh per million output tokens is the index's range, from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on 1 × B200 to Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 on 8 × H100, GPU only. **Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)** is the GPU energy, in watt-hours, that a model on a stated set of GPUs at a stated load uses to generate one million output tokens. One Wh/M equals 0.0036 joules per output token (joules per token × 1,000,000 ÷ 3,600 = Wh/M). On the index the unit runs from **13.0 Wh/M** (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 1 × B200) to **572.9 Wh/M** (Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8, 8 × H100), GPU only, at the most energy-efficient configuration the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 measured for each model and GPU (data compiled 16 February 2026).

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M): definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/#sources)

- **Lowest on the index:** 13.0 Wh/M Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 1 × B200
- **Reference row:** 63.5 Wh/M Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100
- **Highest on the index:** 572.9 Wh/M Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8, 8 × H100

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

The same number reads three ways without conversion: Wh per million tokens equals kWh per billion tokens equals MWh per trillion tokens. The reference row, Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, is 63.5 Wh/M, so a billion of its tokens take 63.5 kWh of GPU energy and a trillion take 63.5 MWh. Multiply by the grid's gCO2e per kWh and divide by 1,000 for kg CO2e per billion tokens: 63.5 × 689 ÷ 1,000 = 43.7 kg on Saudi Arabia's 2024 grid.

The unit is chosen over joules per token because procurement, capacity planning and sustainability reporting all work in watt-hours and tokens, and over watt-hours per query because a query has no fixed length. It is an output-token unit: prompt processing is included in the energy but the prompt's tokens are not in the denominator, which is how the leaderboard measures it. It says nothing about the host, the network, cooling or idle time; see the [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/).

*Where it is used*

## Pages that rely on this term

- [Every model page](https://leadgreen.ai/models/)
- [How much energy does an AI query use?](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### What does Wh/M mean?

Watt-hours per million output tokens: the GPU energy a serving configuration uses to generate a million output tokens. One Wh/M is 0.0036 joules per token. The index runs from 13.0 to 572.9 Wh/M across 32 rows and 18 models, GPU only, each row the lowest-energy configuration measured at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency.

### How do I convert joules per token to watt-hours per million tokens?

Multiply joules per token by 1,000,000 and divide by 3,600. The reference row's 0.2285 J per token becomes 63.5 Wh/M. The reverse is Wh/M × 0.0036 = J per token.

### Is Wh per million tokens the same as kWh per billion tokens?

Yes, and the same as MWh per trillion tokens; the three scale together. 63.5 Wh/M is 63.5 kWh per billion and 63.5 MWh per trillion output tokens.

### Does the unit include the prompt?

The energy includes prompt processing, because the benchmark divides steady-state GPU energy by the output tokens generated in the window; the denominator counts output tokens only. A long-prompt workload therefore shows a higher Wh/M than a short-prompt one for the same answers.

# Energy per token

> 0.047 to 2.06 joules per output token is the index's range of GPU energy per token; 1 Wh per million tokens equals 0.0036 J per token.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

0.047 to 2.06 joules per output token is the index's range of GPU energy per token; 1 Wh per million tokens equals 0.0036 J per token. **Energy per token** is the GPU energy a serving system uses divided by the output tokens it generated in the same window, in joules per output token. The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 measures it as steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the steady-state window, read from the device with Zeus under vLLM on H100 and B200 servers (data compiled 16 February 2026). On the index it runs from **0.047 J per token** (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 1 × B200) to **2.06 J** (Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8, 8 × H100); the index shows it as watt-hours per million output tokens.

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Energy per token: definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/#sources)

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

Energy per token is average power divided by token throughput: on the reference row, 1,177.9 W summed across 2 cards ÷ 5,155.5 output tokens per second = 0.2285 J per token, which is 63.47 Wh/M. The identity is also the consistency check the [RFP scoring box](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/) applies to a bidder's figure.

Three ways of getting the number are not equal. A measured figure reads the GPU's energy counter (NVIDIA NVML or DCGM, which Zeus uses) over a window of steady load and divides by the tokens served. A whole-system figure reads the server's power supplies and includes host, memory, network and fans, which on a DGX B200 adds about 1.79× to the GPU figure. An estimate multiplies a rated power (TDP) by an assumed utilisation and divides by an assumed throughput; it is the kind most often quoted and the kind the index does not publish. Energy per token falls as the running batch rises because the cards' fixed draw is spread over more tokens: see [running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/).

*Where it is used*

## Pages that rely on this term

- [The index method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method)
- [Why it matters: utilisation](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#utilisation)
- [The measurement protocol](https://leadgreen.ai/contribute/#protocol)

Other terms:

- [Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/)
- [Running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/)
- [Floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/)
- [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/)
- [Location-based grid intensity](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/)
- [kg CO2e per billion output tokens](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/)
- [Inter-token latency ceiling](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/)
- [Power usage effectiveness (PUE)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### What is energy per token?

GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the same steady-state window, in joules per output token. The index measures it from the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 and shows it as watt-hours per million output tokens; it runs from 0.047 to 2.06 J per token across the index rows.

### How is energy per token measured?

By reading the GPU's energy counter (through NVML or DCGM; the leaderboard uses Zeus) at the start and end of a steady-state window under a fixed load, and dividing the difference by the output tokens generated in that window. The index's protocol asks for a window of at least 5 minutes after warm-up and at least 1,000 requests. Average power divided by tokens per second gives the same number.

### Why do estimates of energy per token differ so much from measurements?

Estimates multiply a rated power by an assumed utilisation and divide by an assumed throughput, usually a single request at a time. A busy server serves hundreds of requests at once on nearly the same power: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 moves 7.1× in energy per token between a running batch of 8 and 256. An estimate at one request per card lands far above every measured busy-server row.

### Does energy per token include the host, the network and cooling?

Not on this index. The figures are GPU energy only. A whole-system reading adds the host, memory, network and fans (about 1.79× for a DGX B200, from NVIDIA's rated system and GPU power), and the facility's PUE adds cooling and distribution on top.

# Running batch

> Raising the running batch of Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 from 8 to 256 cuts GPU energy from 452.0 to 63.5 Wh per million tokens, 7.1× on the same cards.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

Raising the running batch of Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 from 8 to 256 cuts GPU energy from 452.0 to 63.5 Wh per million tokens, 7.1× on the same cards. **Running batch** is the average number of requests a serving engine was actually decoding at the same time over the steady-state window, which vLLM reports as `num_requests_running`. It is not the cap the operator set (vLLM's `max_num_seqs`) and it does not count requests waiting in the queue. The scheduling that keeps it high is continuous batching, also called in-flight batching: requests join and leave the batch at every decode step, and the running batch is the average that scheduler actually held over the window. On the index, raising the running batch of Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 from **8 to 256** cuts energy per token from **452 to 63.5 Wh/M**, 7.1× on the same hardware (ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0, Text Conversation, data compiled 16 February 2026).

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Running batch: definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/#sources)

- **Lightly loaded:** 452 Wh/M Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100, running batch 8
- **Busy:** 63.5 Wh/M Same model, same cards, running batch 256
- **Same hardware:** 7.1 × Power up 39 percent, throughput up 9.9×

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

The mechanism is fixed draw spread over more work. Between those two rows the cards' power rises 39 percent, from 850 W to 1,178 W, while output throughput rises 9.9×, from 522 to 5,155 tokens per second. Energy per token is power over throughput, so it falls by nearly the whole throughput gain. Median inter-token latency rises from 15 ms to 44 ms over the same range, far under the 500 ms ceiling.

Running batch, not cap, is the figure to ask a vendor for, because a cap of 256 with eight users is a running batch of eight. The [RFP clause](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/) asks for both, and the index's [protocol](https://leadgreen.ai/contribute/#protocol) reports both. The full ladder, 9 configurations, is on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#concurrency) and the [model's page](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-32b/).

*Where it is used*

- [Why it matters: utilisation](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#utilisation)
- [The RFP clause](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/)

- [Floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### What is running batch?

The average number of requests a serving engine was decoding at once over the measurement window (vLLM's num_requests_running). It is not the configured cap and it excludes queued requests. The index reports it on every row because it is the variable that moves energy per token most: 7.1× for Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 between 8 and 256.

### Is running batch the same as continuous batching?

Continuous batching, also called in-flight batching, is the scheduling: requests join and leave the batch at every decode step instead of waiting for a fixed group to finish. Running batch is the measurement: how many requests that scheduler held at once, averaged over the steady-state window. The index reports the second because it is what sets energy per token; the first is how vLLM, TensorRT-LLM and SGLang reach it.

### Why does an idle GPU use more energy per token than a busy one?

Because a GPU's power does not fall in step with its work. On the index, Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 draws 850 W serving 8 requests at once and 1,178 W serving 256, 39 percent more power for 9.9× the tokens per second. Energy per token is power over throughput, so the lightly loaded server uses 7.1× the energy per token: 452 against 63.5 Wh/M. A fully idle GPU produces no tokens, so its energy per token is undefined, and its draw is pure overhead.

### What is the difference between running batch and batch size?

Batch size is usually a configured limit (the cap, vLLM's max_num_seqs) or a fixed count in an offline benchmark. Running batch is what the server actually held on average under a live load, which is lower whenever demand is below the cap. The AI Energy Score's batch size of one is a fixed count; the index's running batch is a measurement.

### What running batch should I ask a vendor to measure at?

The one you expect in production, stated as a number, with the median and p99 inter-token latency your users will accept. The same running batch and latency limit for every bidder makes the figures comparable; the index's rows give the floor to hold each answer against.

*Sources*

# Floor

> Every index row is a floor: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 is 63.5 Wh per million tokens at a running batch of 256, and a real deployment sits above it.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

Every index row is a floor: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 is 63.5 Wh per million tokens at a running batch of 256, and a real deployment sits above it. **A floor** is what every row on the index is: the lowest GPU energy per output token the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 measured for a model on a GPU, among configurations whose median inter-token latency is at or under 500 ms, at high concurrency on a busy server (data compiled 16 February 2026). A real deployment sits above its floor, often far above it: the reference row, Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100, is **63.5 Wh/M** at a running batch of 256, and the same model on the same cards measured **452 Wh/M** at a running batch of 8.

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Floor: definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/#sources)

- **Reference floor:** 63.5 Wh/M Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100, running batch 256
- **Same row, light load:** 452 Wh/M Running batch 8: 7.1× the floor
- **Challenge line:** 10 % below A bidder's figure this far under the floor is asked for its logs

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

The word is chosen so that the rows are read the right way round. A floor is not a typical figure and not a target; it is the best the benchmark found, and it tells a buyer the lowest number a vendor could honestly report for that model on that GPU. An answer below the floor is the one to question: the [RFP scoring box](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/) challenges any figure more than 10 percent under it and asks for the raw power and engine logs.

Floors move with the ceiling that defines them. At 500 ms no measured configuration is excluded; at 250 ms, 1 row changes; at 100 ms, 7 rows change and the lowest becomes Qwen 3 8B on 1 × B200 at 14.7 Wh/M; at 50 ms, 19 rows change and the lowest becomes Qwen 3 8B on 1 × B200 at 17.2 Wh/M and the highest becomes Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 on 8 × H100 at 674.9 Wh/M. None of those tighter ceilings is applied to the index. Above the floors sit every other measured configuration, 328 in all, on the [model pages](https://leadgreen.ai/models/); the highest the leaderboard measured is Llama 3.1 405B Instruct on 8 × B200 at 6,073 Wh/M, holding 8 requests.

*Where it is used*

## Pages that rely on this term

- [The index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/)
- [The index method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method)
- [Scoring RFP answers](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/)

Other terms:

- [Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/)
- [Energy per token](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/)
- [Running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/)
- [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/)
- [Location-based grid intensity](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/)
- [kg CO2e per billion output tokens](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/)
- [Inter-token latency ceiling](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/)
- [Power usage effectiveness (PUE)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### What does the index mean by a floor?

The lowest GPU energy per output token measured for a model and GPU among configurations at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, at high concurrency. Every index row is one. A deployment sits above its floor; Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 is 63.5 Wh/M at its floor and 452 Wh/M at a running batch of 8.

### Is the floor what my deployment will use?

No. It is the best measured configuration on a busy server, GPU only. Your figure depends on your running batch, your prompt and answer lengths, your precision and your card count, and sits above the floor; the model pages show how far above at each measured load.

### What should I do with a vendor figure below the floor?

Ask for the measurement: the running batch held, the latency over the window, the method, the tool and the logs. The index's scoring method challenges any answer more than 10 percent below the floor for the same model and GPU; the measurement protocol's own repeat threshold is 5 percent.

### Does the floor change if the latency ceiling changes?

It can. At 500 ms, the leaderboard's default, no measured configuration is excluded. At 250 ms, 1 row changes; at 100 ms, 7 rows change and the lowest becomes Qwen 3 8B on 1 × B200 at 14.7 Wh/M; at 50 ms, 19 rows change and the lowest becomes Qwen 3 8B on 1 × B200 at 17.2 Wh/M and the highest becomes Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 on 8 × H100 at 674.9 Wh/M. The index applies none of them.

# GPU-only boundary

> The measurement boundary of every index row: energy read from the GPUs alone, with host, network, cooling, idle time and embodied carbon outside it.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

Every index row counts the GPUs alone; in Google's August 2025 disclosure accelerators were 58 percent of a prompt's energy, and the rest sits outside this boundary. **The GPU-only boundary** is the measurement boundary of every index row: energy read from the GPU devices themselves over the steady-state window, with the host CPU and memory, the network and storage, cooling and the rest of the facility, time the GPU spends idle between requests, and the carbon embodied in the hardware all outside it. Google's August 2025 disclosure shows the size of what sits outside: accelerators were **58 percent** of its 0.24 Wh median prompt, and NVIDIA rates a DGX B200 at 14.3 kW against 8.0 kW for its 8 GPUs, a system-to-GPU ratio of **1.79**.

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. GPU-only boundary: definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/#sources)

- **Accelerator share:** 58 % of Google's 0.24 Wh median prompt, August 2025
- **System to GPU:** 1.79 × DGX B200: 14.3 kW rated against 8.0 kW of GPUs
- **At the meter:** 148 Wh/M Reference row × 1.79 × PUE 1.3; illustration, not a measurement

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

Two multipliers take a GPU figure to the facility meter, and both belong to the operator. The system-to-GPU power ratio covers the host, memory, network and fans; the site's power usage effectiveness ([PUE](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/)) covers cooling and distribution. As an illustration, with the DGX B200 ratio of 1.79 and a PUE of 1.3, the reference row's 63.5 Wh/M becomes about 148 Wh/M at the meter, and a gigawatt-hour at the meter serves about 6.8 billion tokens instead of 15.8 billion per megawatt-hour of GPU energy. The PUE is the operator's own figure and the index publishes none.

The boundary is drawn at the GPU because it is the only part a buyer can measure, compare across vendors and hold a vendor to; the rest depends on the site. For scale on embodied carbon, NVIDIA's cradle-to-gate footprint for one HGX B200 baseboard, eight GPUs, is 2,274 kg CO2e. Water is outside the boundary too: the index measures electricity, and the only public per-prompt water figures are Google's 0.26 mL and Mistral's 45 mL per reply.

*Where it is used*

## Pages that rely on this term

- [The index method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method)
- [How much energy does an AI query use?](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/)
- [Why it matters: power](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#power)

Other terms:

- [Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/)
- [Energy per token](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/)
- [Running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/)
- [Floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/)
- [Location-based grid intensity](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/)
- [kg CO2e per billion output tokens](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/)
- [Inter-token latency ceiling](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/)
- [Power usage effectiveness (PUE)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### What does GPU-only mean on the index?

That the energy was read from the GPU devices alone over a steady-state window. Host, network, storage, cooling, idle time between requests and embodied carbon are not counted. Google's August 2025 figures show accelerators at 58 percent of a prompt's whole-stack energy.

### How do I take a GPU-only figure to the facility meter?

Multiply by the system-to-GPU power ratio (1.79 for a DGX B200: 14.3 kW rated against 8.0 kW of GPUs) and by the site's PUE. With a PUE of 1.3, 63.5 Wh/M at the GPU is about 148 Wh/M at the meter. Both multipliers are the operator's own.

### Why not publish whole-system figures?

Because they cannot be compared across vendors or sites: the host, the fans and the cooling design differ with every server and building, while the GPU figure for a named model on a named card at a stated load can be measured anywhere. The index publishes the comparable part and names the multipliers for the rest.

### Does the boundary include the energy of processing the prompt?

Yes. The benchmark divides steady-state GPU energy, which includes prefill, by the output tokens generated; the prompt's tokens are not in the denominator.
