# Location-based grid intensity

> The average carbon intensity of the electricity generated where a GPU runs, in gCO2e per kWh; the factor that turns energy per token into carbon per token.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

689 gCO2e per kWh for Saudi Arabia, 707 for India, 30 for Norway and 473 for the world (2024, Ember): the grid factor that turns energy per token into carbon. **Location-based grid intensity** is the average carbon intensity of the electricity generated in the area where a GPU runs, in grams of CO2e per kilowatt-hour, before any contracts, certificates or self-generation are considered. The index uses Ember's yearly figures (October 2026 release, 2024, the latest year with a value for every listed grid): **689 gCO2e per kWh** for Saudi Arabia, 707 for India, 30 for Norway and 473 for the world. It is a lifecycle figure on net generation, production-based, so upstream methane and plant manufacture are in and imports are out.

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Location-based grid intensity: definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/#sources)

- **Saudi Arabia:** 689 gCO2e/kWh Ember, 2024, lifecycle, location-based
- **World:** 473 gCO2e/kWh Ember, 2024
- **Norway:** 30 gCO2e/kWh 23× cleaner than Saudi Arabia for the same tokens

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

Energy per token does not change with geography; carbon per token does. The reference row's 63.5 Wh/M carries 43.7 kg CO2e per billion tokens on Saudi Arabia's grid and 1.9 kg on Norway's, 23× apart for the same tokens on the same GPUs. Across the 193 grids Ember covers the spread is 55.6×, from Ethiopia at 23.5 to Turkmenistan at 1,306.2 gCO2e per kWh.

Location-based is the method ESRS E1-6 and the GHG Protocol pair with market-based, which uses the supply you contracted (certificates, power purchase agreements) and needs your own figures. Ember's number is for comparing places, not for filing as a Scope 2 combustion factor: a GPU server draws much the same power around the clock while an annual average weights each hour by its generation, so on a grid whose clean supply peaks at midday a flat load sees a higher figure than the average. One page per listed grid is under [Grids](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/), and every grid is in [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json).

*Where it is used*

## Pages that rely on this term

- [Grids](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/)
- [The carbon table](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#carbon)
- [Why it matters: location](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#location)

Other terms:

- [Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/)
- [Energy per token](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/)
- [Running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/)
- [Floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/)
- [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/)
- [kg CO2e per billion output tokens](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/)
- [Inter-token latency ceiling](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/)
- [Power usage effectiveness (PUE)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### What is location-based grid carbon intensity?

The average carbon intensity of the electricity generated where the load runs, in gCO2e per kWh, before contracts or certificates. The index uses Ember's yearly figures (October 2026 release, 2024): Saudi Arabia 689, India 707, Norway 30, world 473.

### What is the difference between location-based and market-based?

Location-based uses the average intensity of the grid where the electricity was consumed. Market-based uses the intensity of the supply you contracted, through certificates or power purchase agreements, and needs your own contract data. ESRS E1-6 asks for both; the index can supply only the first.

### How much does location change the carbon of AI inference?

On the reference row, 23× between Saudi Arabia (43.7 kg CO2e per billion tokens) and Norway (1.9 kg), 2024 averages. The energy figure is identical in both places.

### Can I file Ember's figure in my Scope 2 report?

Use it for comparison, not as the filed factor. It is a lifecycle, production-based figure on net generation, not a Scope 2 combustion factor, and it is an annual average that a round-the-clock GPU load does not follow hour by hour.

# kg CO2e per billion output tokens

> 43.7 kg CO2e per billion output tokens for Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 on Saudi Arabia's grid: Wh per million tokens × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

43.7 kg CO2e per billion output tokens for Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 on Saudi Arabia's grid: Wh per million tokens × gCO2e per kWh ÷ 1,000. **Kilograms of CO2e per billion output tokens** is the carbon unit of the index. It is watt-hours per million output tokens multiplied by the grid's grams of CO2e per kilowatt-hour, divided by 1,000: Wh/M × gCO2e/kWh ÷ 1,000 = kg CO2e per billion tokens, which is also grams of CO2e per million tokens. On the reference row, Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 at 63.5 Wh/M, a billion output tokens carries about **43.7 kg CO2e** on Saudi Arabia's 2024 grid (689 gCO2e/kWh, Ember), **44.9 kg** on India's (707), 30.0 kg on the world average (473) and 1.9 kg on Norway's (30). GPU energy only.

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. kg CO2e per billion output tokens: definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/#sources)

- **Saudi Arabia:** 43.7 kg / bn tokens Reference row × 689 gCO2e/kWh, 2024
- **India:** 44.9 kg / bn tokens Reference row × 707 gCO2e/kWh
- **Norway:** 1.9 kg / bn tokens Reference row × 30 gCO2e/kWh

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

The arithmetic as printed: 63.5 × 689 ÷ 1,000 = 43.7. Across the index the range on Saudi Arabia's grid is 8.9 kg (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, 1 × B200) to 394.8 kg (Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8, 8 × H100) per billion tokens. Per million tokens, read the same numbers in grams: about 43.7 g for the reference row in Saudi Arabia.

The unit is a floor on two counts: the energy is a busy-server GPU-only figure and the grid factor is a location-based annual average. A lightly loaded server multiplies the first factor by several times (7.1× on the reference model's own ladder), and host, network and cooling add to it. Figures per billion are chosen because enterprise token volumes are counted in billions a month; the [grid pages](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) price every index row on each listed grid, and the [MCP server](https://leadgreen.ai/mcp/) prices any configuration on any grid for a token count.

*Where it is used*

- [Grids](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/)
- [Why it matters: the SCI](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#sci)

Other terms:

- [Energy per token](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/)
- [Running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/)
- [Floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/)

- [Power usage effectiveness (PUE)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### How much CO2 does a million AI tokens produce?

On the index's reference row (Qwen 3 32B, 2 × H100, 63.5 Wh per million output tokens, GPU only), about 43.7 g CO2e per million tokens on Saudi Arabia's 2024 grid, 44.9 g on India's, 30.0 g on the world average and 1.9 g on Norway's. Per billion tokens, the same numbers in kilograms.

### How do I calculate kg CO2e per billion tokens?

Multiply watt-hours per million output tokens by the grid's gCO2e per kWh and divide by 1,000. Example: 63.5 Wh/M × 689 gCO2e/kWh ÷ 1,000 = 43.7 kg CO2e per billion tokens.

### Why are some published figures thousands of times higher?

Usually because they start from an estimate of energy per token for a single request at a time, or from a whole-stack figure, and then multiply by a grid factor. The index's energy figures are measured on a busy server, GPU only; at the same grid factor they land far lower. State the boundary and the load before comparing two carbon figures.

### Is this a Scope 2 figure?

It is a location-based GPU-side figure for comparison. GPUs you run put their electricity in your own Scope 2 (ESRS E1-6, location-based matches this method; market-based needs your contracts). Tokens bought from a hosted API are the provider's Scope 2 and your Scope 3, category 1.

*Sources*

## Where every figure came from

Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).

# Inter-token latency ceiling

> 500 ms median inter-token latency is the ceiling an index row must meet; the slowest measured row is 326 ms, so today it excludes nothing.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

500 ms median inter-token latency is the ceiling an index row must meet; the slowest measured row is 326 ms, so today it excludes nothing. **The inter-token latency ceiling** is the limit that decides which measured configurations may be an index row: the median time between one output token and the next must be at or under **500 ms**, the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's own default for every LLM task. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU under that ceiling. No measured configuration reaches it (the slowest Text Conversation row is 326 ms), so at 500 ms the ceiling excludes nothing; it is stated because any energy figure needs the latency it was measured at.

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Inter-token latency ceiling: definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/#sources)

- **Ceiling:** 500 ms median ITL The leaderboard's default for every LLM task
- **Slowest measured row:** 326 ms Text Conversation; the ceiling excludes nothing at 500 ms
- **Reference row:** 44 ms median p99 148 ms at a running batch of 256

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

Energy and latency trade against each other through the running batch: more requests in flight means more tokens per joule and a longer wait between each user's tokens. On the reference model's ladder, median inter-token latency rises from 15 ms at a running batch of 8 to 44 ms at 256 while energy per token falls 7.1×. The reference row's p99 is 148 ms.

Tighter ceilings would change rows: at 250 ms, 1 row changes; at 100 ms, 7 rows change and the lowest becomes Qwen 3 8B on 1 × B200 at 14.7 Wh/M; at 50 ms, 19 rows change and the lowest becomes Qwen 3 8B on 1 × B200 at 17.2 Wh/M and the highest becomes Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 on 8 × H100 at 674.9 Wh/M. None of these is applied to the index; they are reported under [Method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method) so a reader with a stricter requirement can see what moves. In an RFP, fill the ceiling with the latency your users will accept, state it once and use it for every bidder; the [clause](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/) asks for median and p99 over the same window as the energy figure.

*Where it is used*

## Pages that rely on this term

- [The index method](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method)
- [The concurrency ladder](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#concurrency)
- [The RFP clause](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/)

Other terms:

- [Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/)
- [Energy per token](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/)
- [Running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/)
- [Floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/)
- [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/)
- [Location-based grid intensity](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/)
- [kg CO2e per billion output tokens](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/)
- [Power usage effectiveness (PUE)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### What is the inter-token latency ceiling on the index?

A median inter-token latency of at most 500 ms, the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's default for every LLM task. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under it. No measured configuration reaches it, so at this value it excludes nothing.

### What is inter-token latency?

The time between one output token and the next for a single request while the model is generating, usually reported as a median and a p99 over a window. On the reference model's ladder it runs from 15 ms at a running batch of 8 to 44 ms at 256.

### Would a stricter latency limit change the index?

Yes. At 250 ms, 1 row changes; at 100 ms, 7 rows change and the lowest becomes Qwen 3 8B on 1 × B200 at 14.7 Wh/M; at 50 ms, 19 rows change and the lowest becomes Qwen 3 8B on 1 × B200 at 17.2 Wh/M and the highest becomes Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 on 8 × H100 at 674.9 Wh/M. The index applies none of these; they are reported so that a reader with a stricter requirement can see which rows move.

### Why state a latency ceiling with an energy figure at all?

Because energy per token falls as the running batch rises and latency rises with it; a figure without its latency can be made arbitrarily good by loading the server until users wait. The ceiling fixes the trade so that two figures can be compared.

*Sources*

# Power usage effectiveness (PUE)

> Total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy, per ISO/IEC 30134-2; the operator's own multiplier that takes a GPU figure to the building's meter.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Glossary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/)*

The index publishes no PUE: its figures stop at the GPU; PUE, facility energy ÷ IT energy per ISO/IEC 30134-2, is the operator's own multiplier to the meter. **Power usage effectiveness (PUE)** is a data centre's total facility energy divided by the energy delivered to its IT equipment, as defined in ISO/IEC 30134-2. A PUE of 1.0 would mean no energy for cooling, power distribution or lighting; real sites sit above it, and the figure is the operator's own, measured at the building. The index publishes no PUE. It names it because PUE is the second of two multipliers that take a GPU-only figure to the meter: with a system-to-GPU power ratio of 1.79 (DGX B200) and an illustrative PUE of **1.3**, the reference row's 63.5 Wh/M at the GPU becomes about **148 Wh/M** at the facility meter.

**Data** [index.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/index.json), [grid.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/grid.json), [hardware.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/hardware.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Power usage effectiveness (PUE): definition and the figure. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The working](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/#working)
- [Where it is used](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/#used)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/#sources)

- **Illustrative PUE:** 1.3  A stated assumption; the operator's figure is the only real one
- **System to GPU:** 1.79 × DGX B200, NVIDIA rated power
- **Reference row at the meter:** 148 Wh/M 63.5 × 1.79 × 1.3

*The working*

## How the term is used on the index

The arithmetic as printed: 63.5 × 1.79 × 1.3 = 148. The order of the two multipliers does not matter; what matters is that both are stated. A contracted feed then becomes a token capacity: at that figure a gigawatt-hour at the meter serves about 6.8 billion output tokens of the reference row, against 15.8 billion per megawatt-hour of GPU energy.

PUE is a facility metric and says nothing about how much useful work the IT equipment did; a site with a PUE of 1.1 serving eight requests per GPU wastes more energy per token than a site at 1.4 serving two hundred and fifty. Under the Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364, data centres with an installed IT power demand of at least 500 kW report PUE and other facility indicators to the European database; none of those indicators is energy per unit of work, which is what the [index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/) adds. The [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/) entry draws the line the multipliers cross.

*Where it is used*

## Pages that rely on this term

- [The index method: to the meter](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#method)
- [Why it matters: power](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#power)
- [Why it matters: the regulator](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#regulator)

Other terms:

- [Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/)
- [Energy per token](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/)
- [Running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/)
- [Floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/)
- [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/)
- [Location-based grid intensity](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/)
- [kg CO2e per billion output tokens](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/)
- [Inter-token latency ceiling](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/)

*Questions*

## Asked about this term

### What is PUE?

Power usage effectiveness: a data centre's total facility energy divided by the energy delivered to its IT equipment, per ISO/IEC 30134-2. It is measured by the operator at the building and the index publishes none; it is one of the two multipliers that take a GPU-only energy figure to the meter.

### How do I use PUE with watt-hours per million tokens?

Multiply the GPU figure by the system-to-GPU power ratio and by the PUE. Illustration: 63.5 Wh/M × 1.79 (DGX B200) × 1.3 = about 148 Wh/M at the facility meter. Use your own site's PUE and your own server's ratio.

### Does a low PUE mean efficient AI inference?

No. PUE measures the building's overhead, not the work the GPUs did. A site with a low PUE serving few requests per GPU uses more energy per token than a site with a higher PUE whose GPUs are busy. Energy per token measures the work; PUE measures the building.

### Which regulation asks for PUE?

In the EU, the Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791, Article 12, with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364: data centres with an installed IT power demand of at least 500 kW report facility indicators including PUE. No regulation asks for energy per token.

# The nine terms behind the index

> Nine defined terms behind the index, one page each with the figure and the source: Wh per million tokens, energy per token, running batch, floor, PUE.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*Glossary*

Every figure on this site depends on a handful of defined terms: the unit, the boundary, the load, the latency limit and the carbon factor. Each has one page that states the definition, the figure and the source in its first paragraph, with the working underneath. Read them once and every row on the index reads the same way.

**Unit** watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M). GPU only, busy server. Every row is a floor. Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Glossary: the terms behind GPU energy per token. https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

*Terms*

## One page each  Term

### [Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/watt-hours-per-million-output-tokens/)

The unit of the index: the GPU energy, in watt-hours, that a serving configuration uses to generate one million output tokens. Term

### [Energy per token](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/energy-per-token/)

GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the same steady-state window, in joules per token; the quantity the index converts to Wh/M. Term

### [Running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/)

The average number of requests a serving engine was decoding at once over the measurement window, under continuous batching; the variable that moves energy per token most. Term

### [Floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/)

What every index row is: the lowest GPU energy per token measured for a model and GPU under the latency ceiling, which a real deployment sits above. Term

### [GPU-only boundary](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/gpu-only-boundary/)

The measurement boundary of every index row: energy read from the GPUs alone, with host, network, cooling, idle time and embodied carbon outside it. Term

### [Location-based grid intensity](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/location-based-intensity/)

The average carbon intensity of the electricity generated where a GPU runs, in gCO2e per kWh; the factor that turns energy per token into carbon per token. Term

### [kg CO2e per billion output tokens](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/kg-co2e-per-billion-tokens/)

The carbon unit of the index: energy per million tokens multiplied by the grid's carbon intensity, which gives kilograms of CO2e per billion output tokens. Term

### [Inter-token latency ceiling](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/inter-token-latency-ceiling/)

The latency limit that defines which configurations may be an index row: a median inter-token latency at or under 500 ms, the leaderboard's own default. Term

### [Power usage effectiveness (PUE)](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/pue/)

Total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy, per ISO/IEC 30134-2; the operator's own multiplier that takes a GPU figure to the building's meter.

Each term's page carries its own FAQ and sources, and a Markdown copy at its URL followed by `index.md`. The terms are also the vocabulary of the [measurement protocol](https://leadgreen.ai/contribute/#protocol) and the [RFP clause](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/).

# Llama 3.1 8B Instruct vs Llama 3.3 70B Instruct: GPU energy per million output tokens

> Llama 3.3 70B Instruct against Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on GPU energy per output token: 6.03× on the H100 and 4.68× on the B200, from the index rows.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-1-8b-instruct-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-1-8b-instruct-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Compare](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/) · Two sizes · H100 and B200*

On the index rows, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct uses **6.03×** the GPU energy per output token of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on the H100 (117.5 against 19.5 Wh/M, on four cards and one card at running batches of 724 and 511) and **4.68×** on the B200 (60.7 against 13.0 Wh/M, on two cards and one card at running batches of 1,022 and 2,043), GPU only, each at the most energy-efficient configuration the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 measured for it (data compiled 16 February 2026). Llama 3.1 8B Instruct has 8 B parameters; Llama 3.3 70B Instruct has 70 B parameters. Part of each gap is the sweep rather than the model: the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch, and the table states both.

**Unit** watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M). GPU only, busy server. Every row is a floor. **Data** [llama-3-1-8b-instruct.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/models/llama-3-1-8b-instruct.json), [llama-3-3-70b-instruct.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/models/llama-3-3-70b-instruct.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

Cite this page: Lead Green, a Katonic project. Llama 3.1 8B Instruct vs Llama 3.3 70B Instruct: GPU energy per million output tokens. https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-1-8b-instruct-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/, release 2026-10-19, retrieved [date]. CC BY 4.0.

- [The rows](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-1-8b-instruct-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/#rows)
- [What explains it](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-1-8b-instruct-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/#why)
- [Questions](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-1-8b-instruct-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/#faq)
- [Sources](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-1-8b-instruct-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/#sources)

- **H100, index rows:** 6.03 × Llama 3.3 70B Instruct 117.5 Wh/M on 4 × H100 against Llama 3.1 8B Instruct 19.5 Wh/M on 1 × H100.
- **B200, index rows:** 4.68 × Llama 3.3 70B Instruct 60.7 Wh/M on 2 × B200 against Llama 3.1 8B Instruct 13.0 Wh/M on 1 × B200.
- **Parameters:** 8.8 × Llama 3.3 70B Instruct 70 B parameters; Llama 3.1 8B Instruct 8 B parameters.

Each ratio compares the two models' index rows on the same GPU: the lowest-energy configuration the leaderboard measured for each, at or under 500 ms median inter-token latency. The ratio is the second model's energy per token over the first's, so a figure under 1 means the second model's row is the lower one. Card count and running batch differ between the rows and are shown in the table.

*The rows*

## Index rows on every GPU both models share

*Index rows for Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, with the configuration behind each and the per-answer and carbon readings*

| GPU | Model | Cards | Precision | Running batch | GPU W | Tokens / s | Wh / M | Output tokens | Wh per answer | kg CO2e / bn tokens, world grid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H100 | [Llama 3.1 8B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-1-8b-instruct/) | 1 × H100 | BF16 | 511 | 688 | 9,806 | 19.5 | 397 | 0.008 | 9.2 |
| H100 | [Llama 3.3 70B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-3-70b-instruct/) | 4 × H100 | BF16 | 724 | 2,546 | 6,018 | 117.5 | 413 | 0.049 | 55.6 |
| B200 | [Llama 3.1 8B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-1-8b-instruct/) | 1 × B200 | BF16 | 2,043 | 691 | 14,799 | 13.0 | 396 | 0.005 | 6.1 |
| B200 | [Llama 3.3 70B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-3-70b-instruct/) | 2 × B200 | BF16 | 1,022 | 1,935 | 8,854 | 60.7 | 409 | 0.025 | 28.7 |

Running batch is the average number of requests the server was decoding at once over the steady-state window (vLLM's `num_requests_running`). GPU W is the measured average power summed across the cards. Wh per answer is Wh/M times the row's own average output length. Carbon uses the world average grid, 473 gCO2e per kWh (Ember, 2024); the [grid pages](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) price every model on each listed grid. Model names link to every measured configuration.

*What explains it*

## Two sizes

The second model has 8.8× the parameters of the first, and a dense model reads every parameter for every output token, so the weights moved per token scale with size and so does the memory needed to hold them. On the H100 the rows sit on one card (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct) and four cards (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct), at running batches of 511 (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct) and 724 (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct). The energy gap on the H100 (6.03×) is smaller than the parameter gap (8.8×), because each row runs at its own card count and running batch, where its fixed draw is spread over its own number of tokens. Size is the largest lever after load; the question for a buyer is whether the task needs the larger model's answers.

Load still moves the number more than either model does: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 spans 7.1× between a running batch of 8 and 256 on the same cards, which is wider than the gap on this page. Pick the model for the task, then run it busy. The [running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/) and [floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/) entries define the terms.

*Questions*

## Asked about Llama 3.1 8B Instruct against Llama 3.3 70B Instruct

### Is Llama 3.1 8B Instruct more energy-efficient than Llama 3.3 70B Instruct?

Yes, on these rows: on the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's index rows, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct uses 6.03× the GPU energy per output token of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on the H100 (117.5 against 19.5 Wh per million output tokens) and 4.68× the GPU energy per output token of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on the B200 (60.7 against 13.0 Wh per million output tokens). These are floors at high load, GPU only, and the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch.

### How much more energy does Llama 3.3 70B Instruct use per million tokens than Llama 3.1 8B Instruct?

The index rows differ by 98.0 Wh/M on the H100 (98.0 kWh per billion tokens) and 47.7 Wh/M on the B200 (47.7 kWh per billion tokens). Per answer, at each row's own average output length, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct costs 0.008 Wh on the H100 and 0.005 Wh on the B200 and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct 0.049 Wh on the H100 and 0.025 Wh on the B200.

### Does the bigger model cost more per answer?

Yes, at these rows: on the H100, 0.008 Wh for Llama 3.1 8B Instruct against 0.049 Wh for Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, using each row's own average output length (397 and 413 tokens). The larger model also needs more cards to hold its weights (1 against 4 on the H100). Whether its answers are worth the difference is a question about the task, not the index.

### Why are the two rows not like for like?

The leaderboard sweeps each model separately: card count, the cap on requests in flight and the precision are chosen per model, and the running batch actually reached differs. On the H100 the rows here ran on 1 and 4 cards at running batches of 511 and 724. The ratio compares the best measured row on each side, not a matched run; every configuration is on the model pages and in the API, so any pair can be re-cut at a matched cap or running batch.

### Where do these figures come from?

The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026, retrieved 26 September 2026), Text Conversation task, GPU energy measured with Zeus under vLLM on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; each row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under 500 ms median inter-token latency. Carbon per billion tokens multiplies the row by the world average grid intensity, 473 gCO2e per kWh (Ember, 2024).

*Sources*

## Where every figure came from

[ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).

Parameters and architecture as the leaderboard records them (total and activated parameters in billions). Carbon: Ember, Yearly electricity data, October 2026 release, world average 2024, CC BY 4.0, retrieved 17 October 2026.

# Llama 3.3 70B Instruct vs Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8: GPU energy per million output tokens

> Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 against Llama 3.3 70B Instruct on GPU energy per output token: 4.88× on the H100 and 5.25× on the B200, from the index rows.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-3-70b-instruct-vs-llama-3-1-405b-instruct-fp8/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/llama-3-3-70b-instruct-vs-llama-3-1-405b-instruct-fp8/index.md). Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Compare](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/) · Two sizes · H100 and B200*

On the index rows, Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 uses **4.88×** the GPU energy per output token of Llama 3.3 70B Instruct on the H100 (572.9 against 117.5 Wh/M, on eight cards and four cards at running batches of 255 and 724) and **5.25×** on the B200 (318.5 against 60.7 Wh/M, on four cards and two cards at running batches of 510 and 1,022), GPU only, each at the most energy-efficient configuration the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 measured for it (data compiled 16 February 2026). Llama 3.3 70B Instruct has 70 B parameters; Llama 3.1 405B Instruct FP8 has 405 B parameters. Part of each gap is the sweep rather than the model: the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch, and the table states both.

# Qwen 3 32B vs Llama 3.3 70B Instruct: GPU energy per million output tokens

> Llama 3.3 70B Instruct against Qwen 3 32B on GPU energy per output token: 1.85× on the H100 and 1.55× on the B200, from the index rows.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/qwen-3-32b-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/qwen-3-32b-vs-llama-3-3-70b-instruct/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Compare](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/) · Two families, two sizes · H100 and B200*

On the index rows, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct uses **1.85×** the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 32B on the H100 (117.5 against 63.5 Wh/M, on four cards and two cards at running batches of 724 and 256) and **1.55×** on the B200 (60.7 against 39.1 Wh/M, on two cards and one card at running batches of 1,022 and 383), GPU only, each at the most energy-efficient configuration the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 measured for it (data compiled 16 February 2026). Qwen 3 32B has 32 B parameters; Llama 3.3 70B Instruct has 70 B parameters. Part of each gap is the sweep rather than the model: the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch, and the table states both.

**Unit** watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M). GPU only, busy server. Every row is a floor. **Data** [qwen-3-32b.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/models/qwen-3-32b.json), [llama-3-3-70b-instruct.json](https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/models/llama-3-3-70b-instruct.json). Updated 19 October 2026.

| B200 | [Llama 3.3 70B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/llama-3-3-70b-instruct/) | 2 × B200 | BF16 | 1,022 | 1,935 | 8,854 | 60.7 | 409 | 0.025 | 28.7 |

Running batch is the average number of requests the server was decoding at once over the steady-state window (vLLM's `num_requests_running`). GPU W is the measured average power summed across the cards. Wh per answer is Wh/M times the row's own average output length. Carbon uses the world average grid, 473 gCO2e per kWh (Ember, 2024); the [grid pages](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) price every model on each listed grid. Model names link to every measured configuration.

*What explains it*

## Two families, two sizes

Two families and two sizes: Qwen 3 32B (32 B parameters, Dense Transformer) against Llama 3.3 70B Instruct (70 B parameters, Dense Transformer), 2.2× the parameters. On the H100 the rows sit on two cards (Qwen 3 32B) and four cards (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct), at running batches of 256 (Qwen 3 32B) and 724 (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct). The energy gap on the H100 (1.85×) is smaller than the parameter gap (2.2×); architecture, vocabulary and the configuration each model was swept at account for the rest. Qwen 3 32B is the index's reference model, so its full ladder of measured loads is on [the index](https://leadgreen.ai/index/#concurrency), and both models' every configuration is on their pages.

Load still moves the number more than either model does: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 spans 7.1× between a running batch of 8 and 256 on the same cards, which is wider than the gap on this page. Pick the model for the task, then run it busy. The [running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/) and [floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/) entries define the terms.

*Questions*

## Asked about Qwen 3 32B against Llama 3.3 70B Instruct

### Is Qwen 3 32B more energy-efficient than Llama 3.3 70B Instruct?

Yes, on these rows: on the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's index rows, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct uses 1.85× the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 32B on the H100 (117.5 against 63.5 Wh per million output tokens) and 1.55× the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 32B on the B200 (60.7 against 39.1 Wh per million output tokens). These are floors at high load, GPU only, and the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch.

### How much more energy does Llama 3.3 70B Instruct use per million tokens than Qwen 3 32B?

The index rows differ by 54.1 Wh/M on the H100 (54.1 kWh per billion tokens) and 21.7 Wh/M on the B200 (21.7 kWh per billion tokens). Per answer, at each row's own average output length, Qwen 3 32B costs 0.040 Wh on the H100 and 0.025 Wh on the B200 and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct 0.049 Wh on the H100 and 0.025 Wh on the B200.

### Does Llama 3.3 70B Instruct cost more per answer than Qwen 3 32B?

At these rows, on the H100: 0.040 Wh for Qwen 3 32B against 0.049 Wh for Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, using each row's own average output length (634 and 413 tokens). The two differ in family and in size (2.2× the parameters), and the rows differ in cards (2 against 4) and running batch, so the per-answer figure is a reading, not a verdict on either architecture.

### Why are the two rows not like for like?

The leaderboard sweeps each model separately: card count, the cap on requests in flight and the precision are chosen per model, and the running batch actually reached differs. On the H100 the rows here ran on 2 and 4 cards at running batches of 256 and 724. The ratio compares the best measured row on each side, not a matched run; every configuration is on the model pages and in the API, so any pair can be re-cut at a matched cap or running batch.

### Where do these figures come from?

The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026, retrieved 26 September 2026), Text Conversation task, GPU energy measured with Zeus under vLLM on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; each row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under 500 ms median inter-token latency. Carbon per billion tokens multiplies the row by the world average grid intensity, 473 gCO2e per kWh (Ember, 2024).

# Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct vs DeepSeek V3.1: GPU energy per million output tokens

> DeepSeek V3.1 against Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct on GPU energy per output token: 2.52× on the B200, from the index rows.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-vs-deepseek-v3-1/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-vs-deepseek-v3-1/index.md). Updated 19 October 2026, data version 2026-10-19. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for the compilation and text; sources keep their own licences. GPU energy only, measured at steady state on a busy server (the most energy-efficient configuration under a latency limit). Host, network, cooling and idle time are not counted. Every figure is a floor; a lightly used server sits well above it. Machine-readable data: https://leadgreen.ai/api/v1/ (see llms.txt).

*[Compare](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/) · Two mixture-of-experts sizes · B200*

On the index rows, DeepSeek V3.1 uses **2.52×** the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct on the B200 (168.4 against 66.7 Wh/M, on eight cards and four cards at running batches of 3,008 and 3,765), GPU only, each at the most energy-efficient configuration the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 measured for it (data compiled 16 February 2026). Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct has 235 B parameters, 22 B active per token; DeepSeek V3.1 has 671 B parameters, 37 B active per token. Part of each gap is the sweep rather than the model: the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch, and the table states both.

*What explains it*

## Two mixture-of-experts sizes

Two mixture-of-experts models of different total size: Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct activates 22 B of 235 B parameters per token, DeepSeek V3.1 37 B of 671 B. Weights read per token scale with the active parameters (1.7× here), memory with the total (2.9×), so the larger model needs more cards to hold its experts and spreads each token's work across them. On the B200 the rows sit on four cards (Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct) and eight cards (DeepSeek V3.1), at running batches of 3,765 (Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct) and 3,008 (DeepSeek V3.1). The index row ratio on the B200 is 2.52×, between the active-parameter gap and the total-parameter gap.

Load still moves the number more than either model does: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 spans 7.1× between a running batch of 8 and 256 on the same cards, which is wider than the gap on this page. Pick the model for the task, then run it busy. The [running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/) and [floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/) entries define the terms.

Model names link to every measured configuration.

*What explains it*

## Dense against mixture of experts

A dense model reads all of its weights for every output token; a mixture-of-experts model routes each token through a few experts and reads only those. Qwen 3 30B A3B Instruct activates 3 B of its 30 B parameters per token; Qwen 3 32B is dense at 32 B. So the mixture-of-experts model reads about 11× fewer weights per token at a similar total size, and on the H100 its index row uses 0.39× less GPU energy per output token (24.7 against 63.5 Wh/M). The whole model must still fit in memory: On the H100 both rows sit on two cards, at running batches of 1,019 (Qwen 3 30B A3B Instruct) and 256 (Qwen 3 32B). The saving is in weights read per token, not in cards.

Load still moves the number more than either model does: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 spans 7.1× between a running batch of 8 and 256 on the same cards, which is wider than the gap on this page. Pick the model for the task, then run it busy. The [running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/) and [floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/) entries define the terms.

*Questions*

Yes, on these rows: on the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's index rows, Qwen 3 32B uses 2.57× the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 30B A3B Instruct on the H100 (63.5 against 24.7 Wh per million output tokens) and 2.49× the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 30B A3B Instruct on the B200 (39.1 against 15.7 Wh per million output tokens). These are floors at high load, GPU only, and the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch.

### How much more energy does Qwen 3 32B use per million tokens than Qwen 3 30B A3B Instruct?

The index rows differ by 38.8 Wh/M on the H100 (38.8 kWh per billion tokens) and 23.4 Wh/M on the B200 (23.4 kWh per billion tokens). Per answer, at each row's own average output length, Qwen 3 30B A3B Instruct costs 0.023 Wh on the H100 and 0.015 Wh on the B200 and Qwen 3 32B 0.040 Wh on the H100 and 0.025 Wh on the B200.

### Does a mixture-of-experts model use less energy per token than a dense one?

At a similar total size, on these rows, yes: Qwen 3 30B A3B Instruct activates 3 B of 30 B parameters per token and its H100 index row uses 24.7 Wh/M against 63.5 for the dense Qwen 3 32B (32 B), 0.39× less. The mixture-of-experts model reads about 11× fewer weights per token; it still needs memory for all of them, so the saving is in energy per token, not in cards.

### Why are the two rows not like for like?

The leaderboard sweeps each model separately: card count, the cap on requests in flight and the precision are chosen per model, and the running batch actually reached differs. On the H100 the rows here ran on 2 and 2 cards at running batches of 1,019 and 256. The ratio compares the best measured row on each side, not a matched run; every configuration is on the model pages and in the API, so any pair can be re-cut at a matched cap or running batch.

# Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8 vs Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct: GPU energy per million output tokens

> Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct vs Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8: 1.47× on the H100 and 0.48× on the B200 on GPU energy per output token, from the index rows.
>
> Lead Green, a Katonic project. Canonical page: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-fp8-vs-qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct/ (this file: https://leadgreen.ai/compare/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-fp8-vs-qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct/index.md). *[Compare](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/) · Two precisions · H100 and B200*

On the index rows, Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct uses **1.47×** the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8 on the H100 (303.5 against 206.0 Wh/M, both on eight cards at running batches of 228 and 511) and **0.48×** on the B200 (66.7 against 139.1 Wh/M, on four cards and two cards at running batches of 3,765 and 256), GPU only, each at the most energy-efficient configuration the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 measured for it (data compiled 16 February 2026). Part of each gap is the sweep rather than the model: the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch, and the table states both.

Each ratio compares the two models' index rows on the same GPU: the lowest-energy configuration the leaderboard measured for each, at or under 500 ms median inter-token latency. The ratio is the second model's energy per token over the first's, so a figure under 1 means the second model's row is the lower one. Card count and running batch differ between the rows and are shown in the table.

*The rows*

## Index rows on every GPU both models share

*Index rows for Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8 and Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct, with the configuration behind each and the per-answer and carbon readings*

| GPU | Model | Cards | Precision | Running batch | GPU W | Tokens / s | Wh / M | Output tokens | Wh per answer | kg CO2e / bn tokens, world grid |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H100 | [Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-fp8/) | 8 × H100 | FP8 | 511 | 3,961 | 5,342 | 206.0 | 881 | 0.182 | 97.4 |
| H100 | [Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct/) | 8 × H100 | BF16 | 228 | 4,038 | 3,696 | 303.5 | 874 | 0.265 | 143.6 |
| B200 | [Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct-fp8/) | 2 × B200 | FP8 | 256 | 1,891 | 3,776 | 139.1 | 876 | 0.122 | 65.8 |
| B200 | [Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct](https://leadgreen.ai/models/qwen-3-235b-a22b-instruct/) | 4 × B200 | BF16 | 3,765 | 3,196 | 13,303 | 66.7 | 874 | 0.058 | 31.6 |

Running batch is the average number of requests the server was decoding at once over the steady-state window (vLLM's `num_requests_running`). GPU W is the measured average power summed across the cards. Wh per answer is Wh/M times the row's own average output length. Carbon uses the world average grid, 473 gCO2e per kWh (Ember, 2024); the [grid pages](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) price every model on each listed grid. Model names link to every measured configuration.

*What explains it*

## Two precisions

The same model weights at two precisions. FP8 stores each weight in one byte and BF16 in two, so an FP8 row moves half the bytes per token from memory and the model fits on fewer cards or leaves more memory for batching. The FP8 row uses less energy per token on the H100 and more on the B200 (H100: FP8 206.0 Wh/M on eight cards at a running batch of 511, BF16 303.5 Wh/M on eight cards at 228; B200: FP8 139.1 Wh/M on two cards at a running batch of 256, BF16 66.7 Wh/M on four cards at 3,765). Where the FP8 row costs more, the reason is in the table: the two rows were swept to different card counts and reached different running batches, and a quieter row carries a higher energy per token whatever its precision. Quantisation is the cheapest energy lever after load, but these rows show it only pays when the serving configuration is matched; the model pages hold every configuration so the pair can be re-cut at the same cards and cap.

Load still moves the number more than either model does: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 spans 7.1× between a running batch of 8 and 256 on the same cards, which is wider than the gap on this page. Pick the model for the task, then run it busy. The [running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/) and [floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/) entries define the terms.

*Questions*

## Asked about Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8 against Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct

### Is Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8 more energy-efficient than Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct?

It depends on the GPU: on the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's index rows, Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct uses 1.47× the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8 on the H100 (303.5 against 206.0 Wh per million output tokens) and 0.48× the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8 on the B200 (66.7 against 139.1 Wh per million output tokens). These are floors at high load, GPU only, and the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch.

### How much more energy does Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct use per million tokens than Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8?

The index rows differ by 97.6 Wh/M on the H100 (97.6 kWh per billion tokens) and 72.3 Wh/M on the B200 (72.3 kWh per billion tokens); where the ratio is under 1, Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct is the lower row. Per answer, at each row's own average output length, Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8 costs 0.182 Wh on the H100 and 0.122 Wh on the B200 and Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct 0.265 Wh on the H100 and 0.058 Wh on the B200.

### Does FP8 save energy compared with BF16 for the same model?

Not consistently on these index rows. On the H100 the FP8 row (Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8) uses 206.0 Wh/M on 8 cards at a running batch of 511 and the BF16 row 303.5 Wh/M on 8 at 228; on the B200 the FP8 row (Qwen 3 235B A22B Instruct FP8) uses 139.1 Wh/M on 2 cards at a running batch of 256 and the BF16 row 66.7 Wh/M on 4 at 3,765. FP8 halves the bytes moved per token and the memory the weights take, but the leaderboard swept the two variants to different card counts and loads, and load moves energy per token more than precision does. A matched run, same cards and same cap, is the comparison to ask a vendor for.

### Why are the two rows not like for like?

The leaderboard sweeps each model separately: card count, the cap on requests in flight and the precision are chosen per model, and the running batch actually reached differs. On the H100 the rows here ran on 8 and 8 cards at running batches of 511 and 228. The ratio compares the best measured row on each side, not a matched run; every configuration is on the model pages and in the API, so any pair can be re-cut at a matched cap or running batch.

### Where do these figures come from?

The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026, retrieved 26 September 2026), Text Conversation task, GPU energy measured with Zeus under vLLM on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; each row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under 500 ms median inter-token latency. Carbon per billion tokens multiplies the row by the world average grid intensity, 473 gCO2e per kWh (Ember, 2024).

*Sources*

## Where every figure came from

[ML.ENERGY Leaderboard](https://ml.energy/leaderboard/) version 3.0 (released 1 December 2025; data compiled 16 February 2026; retrieved 26 September 2026), The ML.ENERGY Initiative, started at SymbioticLab, University of Michigan. Text Conversation task, 328 stable configurations. Energy per token is steady-state GPU energy divided by the output tokens generated in the window, measured with Zeus under vLLM 0.11.1 on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; energy per request is that figure times the average output length. Each index row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under a 500 ms median inter-token latency, the leaderboard's own default ceiling, which no configuration reaches. Apache 2.0 per the [ml-energy/benchmark-v3](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ml-energy/benchmark-v3) dataset card. Cite [Chung et al., The ML.ENERGY Benchmark, NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06371).

Parameters and architecture as the leaderboard records them (total and activated parameters in billions). Carbon: Ember, Yearly electricity data, October 2026 release, world average 2024, CC BY 4.0, retrieved 17 October 2026.

Running batch is the average number of requests the server was decoding at once over the steady-state window (vLLM's `num_requests_running`). GPU W is the measured average power summed across the cards. Wh per answer is Wh/M times the row's own average output length. Carbon uses the world average grid, 473 gCO2e per kWh (Ember, 2024); the [grid pages](https://leadgreen.ai/grids/) price every model on each listed grid. Model names link to every measured configuration.

*What explains it*

## Two families, one size

Two models of the same size class from different families: Qwen 3 8B (8 B parameters, Dense Transformer) against Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (8 B parameters, Dense Transformer). At the same size the energy per token depends on the architecture's depth and width, the vocabulary, the attention design and, on the leaderboard, the configuration swept for each: card count, cap and the running batch reached. On the H100 both rows sit on one card, at running batches of 474 (Qwen 3 8B) and 511 (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct). The gap here is under 12 percent, which is inside what load alone moves; read the ratio with the running batches beside it.

Load still moves the number more than either model does: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 spans 7.1× between a running batch of 8 and 256 on the same cards, which is wider than the gap on this page. Pick the model for the task, then run it busy. The [running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/) and [floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/) entries define the terms.

*Questions*

## Asked about Qwen 3 8B against Llama 3.1 8B Instruct

### Is Qwen 3 8B more energy-efficient than Llama 3.1 8B Instruct?

No, on these rows: on the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's index rows, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct uses 0.97× the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 8B on the H100 (19.5 against 20.0 Wh per million output tokens) and 0.88× the GPU energy per output token of Qwen 3 8B on the B200 (13.0 against 14.7 Wh per million output tokens). These are floors at high load, GPU only, and the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch.

### How much more energy does Llama 3.1 8B Instruct use per million tokens than Qwen 3 8B?

The index rows differ by 0.5 Wh/M on the H100 (0.5 kWh per billion tokens) and 1.8 Wh/M on the B200 (1.8 kWh per billion tokens); where the ratio is under 1, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct is the lower row. Per answer, at each row's own average output length, Qwen 3 8B costs 0.013 Wh on the H100 and 0.010 Wh on the B200 and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct 0.008 Wh on the H100 and 0.005 Wh on the B200.

### Why do two models of the same size differ in energy per token?

Architecture (depth, width, attention design), vocabulary and, on the leaderboard, the configuration swept for each model: card count, cap and the running batch actually reached. On the H100 the rows here ran at running batches of 474 (Qwen 3 8B) and 511 (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct); a quieter row carries a higher energy per token whatever its architecture. The gap is 12 percent at most, inside what load alone moves.

### Why are the two rows not like for like?

The leaderboard sweeps each model separately: card count, the cap on requests in flight and the precision are chosen per model, and the running batch actually reached differs. On the H100 the rows here ran on 1 and 1 cards at running batches of 474 and 511. The ratio compares the best measured row on each side, not a matched run; every configuration is on the model pages and in the API, so any pair can be re-cut at a matched cap or running batch.

### Where do these figures come from?

The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026, retrieved 26 September 2026), Text Conversation task, GPU energy measured with Zeus under vLLM on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; each row is the lowest-energy configuration for its model and GPU at or under 500 ms median inter-token latency. Carbon per billion tokens multiplies the row by the world average grid intensity, 473 gCO2e per kWh (Ember, 2024).

*Sources*

# Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct vs Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8: GPU energy per million output tokens

> Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8 against Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct on GPU energy per output token: 1.44× on the H100, from the index rows.

> Lead Green, a Katonic project. *[Compare](https://leadgreen.ai/compare/) · Two expert counts · H100*

Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct has 109 B parameters, 17 B active per token; Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8 has 400 B parameters, 17 B active per token. *What explains it*

## Two expert counts

Two mixture-of-experts models with the same active parameters per token (17 B) and very different totals: Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct routes across 16 experts (109 B in all), Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8 across 128 (400 B). The work per token is similar; the memory is not, so the larger model needs more cards to hold its experts and spreads each token's work across them. On the H100 the rows sit on four cards (Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct) and eight cards (Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8), at running batches of 473 (Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct) and 383 (Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8). The index row ratio on the H100 is 1.44×: the price of holding the extra experts, at the running batches stated in the table.

Load still moves the number more than either model does: Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 spans 7.1× between a running batch of 8 and 256 on the same cards, which is wider than the gap on this page. Pick the model for the task, then run it busy. The [running batch](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/running-batch/) and [floor](https://leadgreen.ai/glossary/floor/) entries define the terms.

## Asked about Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct against Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8

### Is Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct more energy-efficient than Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8?

Yes, on these rows: on the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's index rows, Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8 uses 1.44× the GPU energy per output token of Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct on the H100 (134.5 against 93.4 Wh per million output tokens). These are floors at high load, GPU only, and the two rows of a pair differ in card count and running batch.

### How much more energy does Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8 use per million tokens than Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct?

The index rows differ by 41.1 Wh/M on the H100 (41.1 kWh per billion tokens). Per answer, at each row's own average output length, Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct costs 0.038 Wh on the H100 and Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8 0.055 Wh on the H100.

### Do more experts cost more energy per token at the same active parameters?

On these rows, yes: with 17 B active parameters each, Llama 4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct FP8 (400 B in all) uses 1.44× the GPU energy per output token of Llama 4 Scout 17B 16E Instruct (109 B) on the H100, 134.5 against 93.4 Wh/M. The extra experts must be held in memory and the token's work spread across more cards (8 against 4), which is the energy the table shows.

### Why are the two rows not like for like?

The leaderboard sweeps each model separately: card count, the cap on requests in flight and the precision are chosen per model, and the running batch actually reached differs. On the H100 the rows here ran on 4 and 8 cards at running batches of 473 and 383. The ratio compares the best measured row on each side, not a matched run; every configuration is on the model pages and in the API, so any pair can be re-cut at a matched cap or running batch.

*5 questions*

## [Lead Green](https://leadgreen.ai/)

### What is Lead Green?

A public index of LLM inference energy per token: the GPU watt-hours it takes to serve a million output tokens, by model, GPU and configuration, with the grid carbon to price it anywhere. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/#faq)

### What unit does the index use?

Watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M); one Wh/M is 0.0036 joules per token. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/#faq)

### Where do the figures come from?

Energy per token from the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026, retrieved 26 September 2026); grid carbon intensity from Ember's yearly electricity data (October 2026 release, 2024); GPU power ceilings from NVIDIA's... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/#faq)

### Is the data open, and how do I get it?

Yes. The compilation and site text are CC BY 4.0 and the sources keep their own licences. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/#faq)

### Who runs and pays for Lead Green?

Lead Green is run and paid for by Katonic, which sells a sovereign AI platform and benefits when buyers ask the questions on this site. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/#faq)

*5 questions*

## [Why it matters](https://leadgreen.ai/why/)

### Does the EU AI Act require reporting the energy used by AI inference?

Not per inference. Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers of general-purpose AI models to keep technical documentation for the AI Office, and Annex XI, section 1, point 2(e) names the model's known or estimated energy consumption: a... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#faq)

### Which line of ESRS E1 does AI inference energy go on?

For GPUs you run, the electricity is energy consumption from own operations under ESRS E1-5 (paragraph 37) and its emissions are Scope 2 under E1-6, location-based and market-based. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#faq)

### Why does an idle GPU use more energy per token than a busy one?

Because the cards' power does not fall in step with their work. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#faq)

### Does where I run AI change its energy per token?

No; it changes the carbon. The same tokens on the same GPUs use the same energy anywhere. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#faq)

### Is the electricity for AI inference expensive?

No, and that is the point. At the reference row and USD 0.10 per kWh the electricity costs about 0.6 cents per million tokens at the floor; a lightly loaded server pays several times that. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/why/#faq)

*6 questions*

## [AI energy in an RFP](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/)

### How do I put AI energy efficiency in an RFP?

Ask every bidder for the same figure at the same load: GPU energy per million output tokens (Wh/M) for each proposed model and serving configuration, measured at steady state on the proposed hardware at a stated average running batch, with... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#faq)

### What unit should an RFP use for AI energy?

GPU watt-hours per million output tokens (Wh/M), GPU energy only, at a stated running batch and latency. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#faq)

### What running batch and latency should the RFP specify?

The running batch you expect in production, as a number [N], and the median [T] and p99 [T99] inter-token latency your users will accept, the same for every bidder. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#faq)

### How do I score a bidder's energy figure?

Gate first: an answer counts only if it carries the figure, the cap and running batch held, median and p99 latency, output tokens per response, tokens per second, average GPU power, the method, the tool, the versions, the date and the... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#faq)

### Can I ask a hosted API provider for energy per token?

Yes, as a fleet-average figure over the preceding quarter at the fleet's actual utilisation, with the boundary stated, the serving regions and their grids named, the sites' PUE and host-to-GPU power ratio given, the rule that allocates a... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#faq)

### Is PUE enough to compare AI vendors on energy?

No. Power usage effectiveness is the building's overhead on top of the IT load; it says nothing about how much work the IT load does. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/rfp/#faq)

*6 questions*

## [Per query](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/)

### How much energy does an AI query use?

About 0.24 to 0.34 Wh across the whole serving stack, by the published figures from Google (0.24 Wh, August 2025), Epoch AI (0.3 Wh, February 2025), OpenAI (0.34 Wh, June 2025) and Microsoft Research (0.31 Wh, a modelled median for a... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#faq)

### Why is Google's 0.24 Wh per prompt higher than the index's figure?

Mostly boundary. Google counts the whole stack: the accelerators are 58 percent of its 0.24 Wh, about 0.14 Wh, with host machines, idle capacity held for peaks and data-centre overhead making up the rest, and it also publishes a narrow... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#faq)

### How do I convert watt-hours per prompt into watt-hours per million tokens?

Divide the energy per answer by the answer's output tokens and multiply by a million: Wh/M = Wh per answer ÷ output tokens × 1,000,000. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#faq)

### Can the AI Energy Score's Wh per 1,000 queries be converted to Wh per million tokens?

No. The AI Energy Score runs one query at a time (batch size 1) with the answer fixed at ten tokens for non-reasoning models, so the arithmetic (tencent/Hunyuan-1.8B-Instruct: 4.2 Wh per 1,000 queries ÷ 1,000 ÷ 10 tokens × 1,000,000 = 420... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#faq)

### Does how busy the server is change the energy of one query?

More than anything else. Qwen 3 32B on 2 × H100 goes from 63.5 Wh/M at a running batch of 256 to 452 Wh/M at 8, 7.1× on the same hardware, because the cards draw only 39 percent more power serving 256 requests than 8. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#faq)

### What about the carbon and water of one query?

Google puts the median Gemini Apps text prompt at 0.03 g CO2e and 0.26 mL of water (August 2025); Mistral puts a 400-token reply from its large model at 1.14 g CO2e and 45 mL (July 2025), without a watt-hour figure. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/per-query/#faq)

*6 questions*

## [H100 vs B200](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/)

### Is the B200 more energy-efficient than the H100 for LLM inference?

On the ML.ENERGY Leaderboard's index rows, yes for all 14 models measured on both: [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#faq)

### How much energy does a B200 save over an H100 per million tokens?

It depends on the model: for the reference model, Qwen 3 32B, the index rows are 63.5 Wh/M on 2 × H100 against 39.1 Wh/M on 1 × B200. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#faq)

### Does the B200 draw more power than the H100?

A B200 card draws more power than an H100: NVIDIA rates the H100 SXM at up to 700 W and the B200 configurable up to 1,000 W, and on these index rows the cards averaged 612 W per H100 and 868 W per B200. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#faq)

### Should I buy B200s to cut the energy of AI inference?

Not first. The same model on the same H100 cards moves 7.1× in energy per token between a running batch of 8 and 256, which is more than the widest generation gap here (4.55×). [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#faq)

### Why do the two rows of a pair have different card counts?

The leaderboard picks each GPU's configurations separately; a B200 has more memory, so a model that needs eight H100s can fit fewer B200s. [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#faq)

### Where do these figures come from?

The ML.ENERGY Leaderboard v3.0 (data compiled 16 February 2026, retrieved 26 September 2026), Text Conversation task, GPU energy measured with Zeus under vLLM on H100 80GB HBM3 and B200 servers; each row is the lowest-energy configuration... [Full answer](https://leadgreen.ai/h100-vs-b200/#faq)
